lectures.title: Nitrogen Balance, Protein Digestion and Transaminases

slides.note: Correction: glutamate is made from α-ketoglutarate (α-KG, a citric acid cycle intermediate) by adding an amino group, not the reverse. Also, the ~30 g/day in the figure is what leaves the pool to build nitrogen-containing compounds (porphyrins such as heme, creatine, neurotransmitters, purines, pyrimidines); the amount of non-essential amino acids made varies. The amino acid pool (~90–100 g of free amino acids in cells and blood) is filled by the three sources on top and emptied by the uses below.

Negative: more nitrogen leaves than comes in, because body protein is broken down faster than it is rebuilt (too little intake, or the catabolic stress of fever, burns or wasting disease). Positive: the body is building new tissue and keeps nitrogen. After starvation the body rebuilds the protein it lost, so the balance turns positive.

Digestion takes two steps. Proteases cut whole proteins into shorter chains (peptides). Peptidases then clip the peptides down to single amino acids. The side lists sort the players by where they are made: stomach (gastric), pancreas or intestine. Names ending in “-ogen” or starting with “pro-” are inactive forms that work only after a piece is cut off. Rennin (chymosin) curdles milk in the stomach of newborn mammals. Do not confuse it with renin, the kidney enzyme that raises blood pressure.

a.a. = amino acid. Endopeptidases cut bonds inside the chain; exopeptidases clip one amino acid off an end (aminopeptidase from the N-terminus, carboxypeptidase from the C-terminus). Zymogens are inactive precursors that switch on only after a piece is cut off, so the pancreas does not digest itself. Pepsinogen is activated by HCl and by pepsin itself. Free amino acids and di- and tripeptides are taken up from the gut lumen into the intestinal cells. The peptides are split there, so only free amino acids pass into the portal blood, which carries them to the liver (“TO LIVER” arrow).

Correction: only trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase are serine proteases; carboxypeptidases A and B are zinc-dependent exopeptidases. Follow the blue arrows: enteropeptidase (also called enterokinase) on the brush border cuts trypsinogen into trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and all the other zymogens, so one trigger starts the whole cascade. Black arrows: each zymogen is cut into its active enzyme. Dotted arrows: the peptide bond each enzyme cuts, with the residues it prefers written above.

Each enzyme cuts the peptide bond on the carboxyl side of (right after) certain residues. Trypsin: basic Arg, Lys. Chymotrypsin: bulky aromatic Phe, Trp, Tyr (plus Met, Leu). Elastase: small Ala, Gly, Ser. Carboxypeptidase removes the last amino acid at the C-terminus: A takes neutral ones (Ala, Ile, Leu, Val), B takes basic ones (Arg, Lys).
Correction: “serine proteases” covers trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase only. Carboxypeptidase is a zinc enzyme, not a serine protease.

The white arrow pointing left is reabsorption: from the proximal tubule fluid back into the blood. The black bar shows it blocked, so cystine, ornithine, arginine and lysine stay in the tubule and leave in the urine (arrow down). Cystine is two cysteines joined by a disulfide bond. It is the only one of the four too insoluble to stay dissolved, so only cystine forms stones; the other three just wash out. The same carrier works in the gut. Lab: hexagonal crystals in the urine. Treatment: plenty of fluids and alkaline urine.

The faulty carrier normally moves neutral amino acids (no net charge, such as Trp) from the gut lumen and from the kidney tubule fluid into the blood. Without it they stay in the gut and the tubule, so they are lost in stool and urine. Losing Trp (tryptophan) is what causes disease, because the body makes part of its niacin (vitamin B3, used to build NAD⁺) from Trp. Low niacin gives pellagra: sun-sensitive dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia or ataxia. Nicotinic acid is niacin, so supplements fix it.

Correction: the C in COAL is cystine (two cysteines joined by a disulfide bond), not single cysteine. Both diseases lose large amounts of amino acids in the urine (gross aminoaciduria), because the carrier that should return them from the kidney tubule fluid to the blood is faulty. Cystine is too insoluble to stay dissolved, so it forms the hexagonal (six-sided) crystals in the photo and then stones. In Hartnup, the crossed arrow means the body is left with too little tryptophan to make niacin, so pellagra-like symptoms appear.

Answer: C. Cystinuria is the most common inherited defect of amino acid transport (1 in 7,000). Its faulty carrier moves the basic amino acids ornithine, arginine and lysine, plus cystine. Hartnup is also a carrier defect, but for neutral amino acids such as tryptophan, and it is rarer (1 in 24,000). OTC (ornithine transcarbamoylase) and CPS-1 (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) are urea cycle enzymes, and albinism is a defect in a pigment-making enzyme, so none of them is a transport protein.

Correction: CFTR is a chloride (Cl⁻) channel; water follows Cl⁻ out of cells. Without it, secretions dry into thick mucus that plugs the pancreatic ducts, so pancreatic enzymes cannot reach the gut. Fat and protein go undigested, giving steatorrhea (bulky, greasy, foul stools). Lab: high sweat Cl⁻. Treatment: pancreatic enzyme pills with meals.

Gliadin (the harmful part of gluten, found in wheat, barley and rye) triggers an immune attack on the small-intestine lining. The villi flatten (villous atrophy), so the absorbing surface shrinks. Lab: IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase. The MHC link is HLA-DQ2/DQ8 (HLA = the human MHC genes).

Breakdown splits an amino acid in two. The amino group (red circle) is passed to another molecule (transamination) and travels in the blood to the liver as glutamine or alanine. It is then freed as ammonia (deamination), and the liver makes the ammonia into urea. The carbon skeleton (blue box) is left as a keto acid. It is burned for energy in the TCA (citric acid) cycle, or made into glucose if it gives pyruvate or a cycle intermediate. Leucine and lysine give only acetyl CoA and its derivatives, so they make ketone bodies, never glucose.

ALT and AST normally sit inside cells. When cells die, the enzymes leak into blood, so high serum levels mean cell damage. Liver holds most of the body's ALT, so ALT is the more liver-specific marker (think ALT = Liver). AST also leaks from damaged heart and skeletal muscle. IU/L = international units of enzyme activity per liter.

Axes: hours after taking the poison (across) and how many times above the upper limit of normal (up). Blue line: ALT leaks from injured liver cells into the blood within hours and peaks at ~20× around 1.5 days, so it is an early marker. Orange line: bilirubin rises only after ~36 h, once so much liver is lost that it can no longer conjugate and excrete bilirubin. Bilirubin then builds up and causes jaundice (yellow skin and eyes).

The top line is the general rule. Amino acid 1 (AA₁) hands its amino group to keto acid 2, so AA₁ becomes keto acid 1 and keto acid 2 becomes amino acid 2. A keto acid is an amino acid's carbon skeleton with C=O in place of the amino group. The double arrows mean each reaction runs both ways, and no free ammonia is released. In both examples the acceptor is α-ketoglutarate, which becomes glutamate. B6 = vitamin B6, which every transaminase needs.

Transamination: only the amino group (red) moves. Alanine becomes its keto acid, pyruvate (green arrow), and α-KG (α-ketoglutarate) becomes glutamate (big blue arrow). Each carbon skeleton keeps its size (3C stays 3C, 5C stays 5C). The reaction runs both ways (red double arrow). SGPT is ALT's old name.

Aspartate gives its amino group to α-KG, making oxaloacetate (OAA) and glutamate. SGOT is AST's old name. The asterisk: during amino acid breakdown AST mostly runs right to left (glutamate + OAA → aspartate + α-KG). Glutamate hands its amino group to OAA, and the aspartate formed carries the second nitrogen into the urea cycle.

Follow the red boxes. In muscle, amino groups from broken-down protein collect on glutamate, and ALT moves them onto pyruvate, making alanine (the middle equation read right to left). Alanine carries the nitrogen through blood to the liver in a non-toxic form. In liver, ALT runs the other way (left to right): alanine gives its amino group to α-KG, becoming pyruvate again and making glutamate. Glutamate dehydrogenase (Glu DH) then frees that amino group as NH₄⁺, which the urea cycle turns into urea. Pyruvate is made into glucose, which returns to muscle through the blood.

PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6) is the cofactor of every aminotransferase. It carries the amino group for a moment, in two steps. Top: glutamate hands its NH₂ (red box) to PLP and becomes α-KG, while PLP becomes pyridoxamine phosphate. Bottom (arrow runs right to left): pyridoxamine phosphate passes the NH₂ to oxaloacetate, making aspartate, and turns back into PLP.

Answer: D. Pyruvate + glutamate → alanine + α-ketoglutarate is the ALT (alanine aminotransferase) reaction run toward alanine, as in muscle. Every aminotransferase needs pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of pyridoxine (vitamin B6), to carry the amino group. Niacin is the tempting wrong choice: it builds NAD⁺ for oxidation-reduction reactions and moves no amino groups. Folic acid, cobalamin (vitamin B12) and tetrahydrobiopterin serve other enzymes.
Answer: C. Saliva has no protease. Protein digestion starts in the stomach with pepsin, continues with pancreatic enzymes and ends with peptidases on the small-intestine brush border.

Answer: C. Enteropeptidase on the brush border makes the first trypsin, and trypsin activates the rest. Trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen are inactive zymogens, pepsinogen belongs to the stomach, and carboxypeptidase activates nothing.

Answer: A. Hartnup blocks uptake of Trp, which the body uses to make niacin; niacin deficiency is pellagra. Cystinuria loses only cystine, ornithine, arginine and lysine, so it causes stones, not pellagra.

Answer: D. ALT leaks from injured liver cells and is the most liver-specific enzyme on the list. Enterokinase (another name for enteropeptidase), pepsin and trypsin are gut digestive enzymes; PLP is a vitamin cofactor, not a marker of injury.

qs.q: Which source adds the most amino acids to the body's free amino acid pool each day?
qs.why: Body protein turnover supplies about 300–400 g/day, compared with about 100 g/day from dietary protein.

qs.q: Glutamate is made by adding an amino group to which citric acid cycle intermediate?
qs.why: α-ketoglutarate plus an amino group gives glutamate. Oxaloacetate plus an amino group gives aspartate instead.

qs.q: What does negative nitrogen balance mean?
opts: No nitrogen is excreted as urea
qs.why: More nitrogen leaves than comes in, because body protein is broken down faster than it is rebuilt. Equal intake and output is nitrogen balance (healthy adult).

qs.q: Which condition produces a positive nitrogen balance?
qs.why: Pregnancy builds new tissue, so the body keeps nitrogen. Fasting, burns and fever break down body protein and cause negative balance.

qs.q: After enteropeptidase makes the first trypsin, what activates the remaining pancreatic zymogens?
qs.why: Trypsin activates more trypsinogen and all the other pancreatic zymogens, so one trigger starts the whole cascade. Enteropeptidase only makes the first trypsin.

qs.q: Trypsin cuts peptide bonds after which residues?
qs.why: Trypsin prefers basic Arg and Lys. Chymotrypsin takes bulky aromatics, elastase small residues, and carboxypeptidase the C-terminal residue.

qs.q: Which pancreatic protease is a zinc-dependent exopeptidase rather than a serine protease?
qs.why: Only trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase use an active-site serine. Carboxypeptidases A and B are zinc enzymes that clip residues off the C-terminus.

qs.q: Why are pancreatic proteases secreted as inactive zymogens?
opts: So the pancreas does not digest itself
So they cut only inside the chain
So they can be absorbed intact
qs.why: Zymogens switch on only after a piece is cut off in the intestine, which protects the pancreas from its own enzymes.

qs.q: Cystinuria causes urinary loss of cystine, ornithine, arginine and lysine. Why does only cystine form stones?
opts: It is the only one filtered by the glomerulus
It is too insoluble to stay dissolved
It is the only one lost in large amounts
It is the only one absorbed from the gut
qs.why: Cystine (two cysteines joined by a disulfide bond) precipitates at high urine concentration; ornithine, arginine and lysine stay dissolved and simply wash out.

qs.q: In Hartnup disorder, poor tryptophan absorption causes deficiency of which vitamin?
qs.why: The body makes part of its niacin from tryptophan, so losing Trp gives pellagra-like dermatitis, diarrhea and neurologic signs; nicotinic acid supplements fix it.

qs.q: CFTR, the protein defective in cystic fibrosis, is a channel for which ion?
qs.why: CFTR moves Cl⁻ and water follows. Without it, thick mucus plugs the pancreatic ducts, so enzymes cannot reach the gut and fat and protein go undigested (steatorrhea).

qs.q: In celiac disease, how does eating gluten reduce nutrient absorption?
opts: An immune attack flattens the intestinal villi
Mucus plugs block the pancreatic ducts
It blocks renal reabsorption of amino acids
qs.why: Gliadin in gluten (wheat, barley, rye) triggers an autoimmune attack on the small-intestine lining; villous atrophy shrinks the absorbing surface. It reverses on a gluten-free diet.

qs.q: Why is AST (aspartate aminotransferase) less specific than ALT (alanine aminotransferase) for liver injury?
opts: AST is cleared from blood within minutes
AST is found only in the bile ducts
AST is also found in heart and skeletal muscle
AST does not leak from dying cells
qs.why: ALT is concentrated mainly in the liver, so a high ALT points to liver. AST also leaks from damaged cardiac and skeletal muscle.

qs.q: After acute toxic liver injury, how do serum ALT and bilirubin change?
opts: Bilirubin rises first; ALT rises later
ALT rises within hours; bilirubin rises later
qs.why: ALT leaks from injured cells early, peaking around 1.5 days. Bilirubin rises only after about 36 h, once too much liver is lost to conjugate and excrete it, causing jaundice.

qs.q: ALT transfers alanine's amino group to α-ketoglutarate. What are the products?
qs.why: Only the amino group moves: alanine becomes its keto acid, pyruvate, and α-ketoglutarate becomes glutamate. Oxaloacetate and glutamate are AST's products.

qs.q: Which α-keto acid corresponds to aspartate?
qs.why: Aspartate (4C) pairs with oxaloacetate (4C); alanine (3C) pairs with pyruvate, and glutamate (5C) with α-ketoglutarate.

qs.q: In the glucose-alanine cycle, muscle ALT transfers amino groups onto which molecule to make alanine?
qs.why: Pyruvate from glycolysis accepts the amino group and becomes alanine, which carries the nitrogen to the liver in a non-toxic form.

qs.q: In the liver, which enzyme releases NH₃ from glutamate so it can be made into urea?
qs.why: ALT moves alanine's amino group onto α-ketoglutarate to form glutamate; glutamate dehydrogenase then frees it as NH₃. Aminotransferases never release free NH₃.

qs.q: In the glucose-alanine cycle, what does the liver make from alanine's carbon skeleton?
qs.why: Alanine becomes pyruvate, which the liver uses for gluconeogenesis; the glucose returns to muscle. Only the nitrogen ends up in urea.

qs.q: Which cofactor do all aminotransferases, including ALT and AST, require?
qs.why: PLP briefly holds the amino group, becoming pyridoxamine phosphate, then hands it to the keto acid and turns back into PLP.

qs.q: Why does enzymatic protein digestion not begin in the mouth?
opts: Salivary protease works only at pH 2
qs.why: Saliva has no protease. Protein digestion starts in the stomach with pepsin, continues with pancreatic enzymes and ends with brush-border peptidases.

qs.q: Enterokinase is another name for which enzyme?
qs.why: Enterokinase is enteropeptidase, the brush-border enzyme that cuts trypsinogen into trypsin to start the zymogen cascade.

qs.q: Which protease precursor is made in the stomach rather than the pancreas?
qs.why: Chief cells of the stomach secrete pepsinogen, which acid and pepsin activate. Trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen and proelastase come from the pancreas.

slides.note: High NH₃ starves the brain of energy. NH₃ is added to α-KG (α-ketoglutarate) to make glutamate (Glu), and to Glu to make glutamine (Gln). Making Glu uses up α-KG, so α-KG is drained from the TCA (citric acid) cycle; with less α-KG, less OAA (oxaloacetate) is made further around the cycle, so ATP falls. Astrocytes store NH₃ as Gln, but Gln is carried into their mitochondria, where mitochondrial glutaminase frees the NH₃ again. That NH₃ triggers ROS (reactive oxygen species), which damage the mitochondria; the astrocytes swell, causing brain edema.

When the liver cannot make urea (red slash through “Liver”), NH₃ rises in the blood. The extra NH₃ is stored as glutamine, so glutamine rises, and BUN falls. BUN (blood urea nitrogen) is the lab measure of urea in blood. Left branch: acquired liver disease, either sudden damage (viral hepatitis, ischemia = loss of blood flow, liver toxins) or chronic cirrhosis, where portal blood from the gut bypasses the liver (portosystemic shunting). Right branch: inherited urea cycle enzyme deficiencies.

Answer: D. In cirrhosis, scar tissue replaces working liver cells, and collateral vessels carry portal blood around the liver. NH₃ from the gut is then not turned into urea, so it builds up in the blood. A is wrong: more arginase would make more urea. E is backwards: a liver that makes less urea gives a low BUN. B and C are not real mechanisms (pepsin digests protein in the stomach; urea is made in the liver).

Breaking down an amino acid splits it into two parts. The amino group (circled) must be disposed of: transamination (most tissues) moves it onto another molecule, deamination (liver, kidney, intestine) frees it as NH₃, and the liver's urea cycle turns NH₃ into urea. Between tissues, nitrogen travels as glutamine or alanine, not as free NH₃. The carbon skeleton (a keto acid) is fuel: it can be burned for energy or made into glucose or ketone bodies. Leucine and lysine give only acetyl CoA and its derivatives, so they make ketone bodies but never glucose.

Blood NH₃ comes mostly from the gut (about half; colon bacteria break down urea and protein) and the kidney (about 40%; it splits glutamine). The kidney sends much of its NH₃ into urine as NH₄⁺ (ammonium), which carries acid out of the body.

ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and AST (aspartate aminotransferase) move the amino group (pink) from an amino acid onto α-KG, making glutamate. They need PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6) and release no free NH₃. Glutamate dehydrogenase then strips the amino group off glutamate as NH₄⁺ (circled) and gives back α-KG.

Top line = the general rule: a transaminase moves the amino group from one amino acid (AA₁) onto a keto acid (a carbon skeleton with C=O where the amino group was), making a new amino acid (AA₂). ALT: alanine + α-KG ⇌ pyruvate + glutamate. AST: aspartate + α-KG ⇌ oxaloacetate + glutamate. Both need vitamin B6 (as PLP) and run in either direction. Read right to left, AST makes the aspartate that later gives urea one of its two nitrogens.

Both enzymes interconvert glutamate and α-KG. The difference is free NH₃. A transaminase (left box; most tissues) passes the amino group to or from another amino acid, so no free NH₃ appears. Glutamate dehydrogenase (right box; liver, kidney, intestine) releases free NH₃ going down (glutamate → α-KG) and takes up free NH₃ going up (α-KG → glutamate).

Top arrow (left to right, uses NAD⁺): glutamate → α-KG + NH₃. This is the liver direction after a protein meal; the NH₃ goes to urea and the α-KG to the TCA cycle (red arrows). Bottom arrow (right to left, uses NADPH): α-KG + NH₃ → glutamate. This traps NH₃ in glutamate when NH₃ is high, as in the brain. The concentrations of the reactants decide the direction.

Glutamate dehydrogenase in its simplest form. Down arrow: glutamate → α-KG + NH₃, while NAD⁺ becomes NADH (oxidative deamination). Up arrow: α-KG + NH₃ → glutamate. The two small red arrows at the left show what happens when NH₃ rises (↑): the reaction is pushed upward and uses up α-KG, so α-KG falls (↓). In the brain this drains α-KG from the TCA cycle, which is why high NH₃ lowers ATP.

Glutamine synthetase (uses ATP) adds NH₃ to glutamate in muscle, brain and other tissues, making glutamine to carry NH₃ safely in blood. Glutaminase (mainly liver, kidney, gut) frees the NH₃ again: the liver turns it into urea, and the kidney excretes it as NH₄⁺. Synthetase traps NH₃; glutaminase releases it.

Glutamine carries two nitrogens, and they come off in two steps. Glutaminase (liver, kidney, intestine) cuts off the side-chain (amide) N as NH₃ and leaves glutamate. Glutamate dehydrogenase then removes glutamate's amino group as a second NH₃ and leaves α-KG. The up arrow on the second step means it can also run backward and take up NH₃ when NH₃ is high.

Many tumors burn glutamine. Glutaminase frees one NH₃ (Gln → Glu), glutamate dehydrogenase (Glu DH) frees a second (Glu → α-KG), and α-KGDH (α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) turns α-KG into succinyl CoA (structures at left) in the TCA cycle to make ATP. Breast cancer cells recycle the NH₃: Glu DH runs the other way (α-KG + NH₃ → glutamate), and that glutamate supplies N for new amino acids.

Left to right: tubule lumen (yellow; fluid that becomes urine), proximal tubule cell, blood (pink). Top row: the cell splits glutamine and frees NH₃, which goes out into the lumen, binds a secreted H⁺ and leaves in urine as NH₄⁺ (ammonium). So the kidney uses glutamine to excrete acid. Inside the cell, CA (carbonic anhydrase) turns CO₂ + H₂O into H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate). The H⁺ is secreted into the lumen in exchange for Na⁺; the HCO₃⁻ goes into the blood. In the lumen, H⁺ plus filtered HCO₃⁻ gives CO₂, which diffuses into the cell (dashed arrow).

Follow nitrogen from the tissues to the urine. Most tissues (circle): transamination puts amino groups on glutamate, and adding NH₃ makes glutamine, which travels in the blood to three places. Kidney (proximal tubule cell): NH₃ is freed, goes into the lumen, binds H⁺ and leaves as NH₄⁺, the minor excreted form. Intestine: NH₃ is freed and goes to the liver. Liver (triangle): NH₃ from glutamine and from glutamate (filled by ALT and AST) becomes urea, the major excreted form. Muscle also sends alanine; the liver turns it into pyruvate, then glucose, which returns to muscle (glucose–alanine cycle).

Answer: C, glutamate dehydrogenase. Oxidative deamination removes glutamate's amino group as free NH₃ and leaves α-KG, while NAD⁺ takes the electrons (the “oxidative” part). In the liver this NH₃ goes into urea. ALT and AST only transfer amino groups, so they free no NH₃. Glutaminase also frees NH₃, but by adding water to glutamine (hydrolysis), with no oxidation. Glutamine synthetase does the opposite: it uses up NH₃.

Each line names the enzymes that act on that step, but not all of them release NH₃. Free NH₃ comes from glutamate dehydrogenase (line 1), glutaminase (line 2), urease, monoamine oxidase and adenosine deaminase. Transaminases only move the amino group onto α-KG to make glutamate, and glutamine synthetase runs the other way, trapping NH₃ in glutamine.
Periportal hepatocytes are the liver cells closest to where portal blood from the gut enters each lobule, so they meet the incoming NH₃ first.

Both urea N atoms come from glutamate: glutamate dehydrogenase frees one as NH₃ (used to make carbamoyl phosphate), and AST moves the other onto oxaloacetate to make aspartate. The carbon comes from CO₂. '4 ATP' means 4 high-energy bonds: 3 ATP are used, but one is split to AMP + PPi (pyrophosphate), which costs 2 bonds. Steps 1–2 run in mitochondria, steps 3–5 in cytosol.

CPS I (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) is the rate-limiting step. It works only when NAG (N-acetylglutamate) binds it as an allosteric activator. Don't confuse it with CPS II, which sits in the cytosol, takes N from glutamine, needs no NAG, and starts pyrimidine synthesis.

Right of the curved membrane = mitochondrial matrix; left = cytosol. OTC (ornithine transcarbamoylase) moves the carbamoyl group, carrying the first N, onto ornithine to make citrulline; the phosphate leaves as Pi (free phosphate). 'No codon' means ornithine and citrulline are never built into proteins. A transporter swaps citrulline out of the mitochondrion into the cytosol for ornithine coming in (white arrows).

ASS (argininosuccinate synthetase) joins citrulline to aspartate. Aspartate's amino group becomes urea's second N. AST supplies the aspartate by moving glutamate's amino group onto OAA (the AST equation read right to left, along the red arrow). Splitting ATP to AMP + PPi spends 2 high-energy bonds; this is the cycle's third and last ATP.

ASL (argininosuccinate lyase) splits argininosuccinate: the N stays on arginine, and aspartate's carbon skeleton leaves as fumarate. In the cytosol, fumarate becomes malate (thin black arrow). Then follow the blue arrows: malate → OAA (by MDHc, cytosolic malate dehydrogenase) → aspartate (by AST), which feeds step 3 again. Malate can instead enter the mitochondria for the TCA cycle. The fumarate route links the urea and TCA cycles.
The kidney has ASS and ASL, so it turns citrulline made by the gut into arginine. It cannot make urea, because only the liver splits arginine into urea with arginase.

The whole cycle. Use the red numbers 1–5 (enzyme steps); the black numbered boxes are separate captions. Shaded right side = mitochondrial matrix (1 CPS1, 2 OTC); left = cytosol (3 ASS, 4 ASL, 5 arginase). Follow the pink N atoms: one enters as free NH₃ at step 1, the other comes from aspartate at step 3. The green C comes from CO₂. These three atoms end up in urea (red box), and ornithine goes back into the mitochondrion to start the next turn.

About 75% of urea travels in the blood to the kidneys and leaves in urine (blue line). About 25% diffuses into the colon (red line), where bacterial urease splits it into NH₃, and the portal vein (green line) carries that NH₃ back to the liver. In kidney failure, blood urea rises, more of it reaches the gut, and the extra NH₃ raises blood ammonia. “Renal aorta” means the renal artery.

Start at the liver box: NH₃ from the body's own tissues (“endogenous”) and from the colon feeds the urea cycle. About 75% of the urea goes to the kidneys. About 25% enters the colon, where bacterial ureases split it back into NH₃; bacteria also free NH₃ from proteins. This NH₃ enters the portal blood: the liver removes about 85%, and about 15% passes into the systemic circulation. NH₃ that picks up H⁺ becomes NH₄⁺ and leaves in feces. Oral neomycin (an antibiotic) kills gut bacteria, so less NH₃ is made, which helps in kidney failure.

BUN rises when the kidneys filter less (kidney disease, dehydration) or when the liver makes more urea from extra amino acids (high-protein diet, tissue breakdown, blood digested after a GI bleed, glucocorticoids breaking down muscle). It falls when the liver makes less urea (liver disease) or less protein comes in.

Short term (feed-forward): more amino acids → more glutamate and arginine → more NAG (N-acetylglutamate) → faster CPS I. Long term: a high-protein diet and fasting both raise the amount of every urea-cycle enzyme. In fasting, glucagon boosts gluconeogenesis from amino acids: alanine from muscle becomes pyruvate in the liver, and its amino group must leave as urea.

The cycle runs in the fed state (amino acids from a protein meal) and in fasting (amino acids from muscle protein), because both bring amino groups to the liver. Steps 1–2 are mitochondrial; steps 3–5 are cytosolic. CPS-I (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) is the rate-limiting step. NAG (N-acetylglutamate) activates it directly; arginine acts one step earlier, by activating the enzyme that makes NAG. Energy cost per urea: 3 ATP, which is 4 high-energy bonds. When the cycle fails, NH₃ builds up (hyperammonemia).

The double bars (//) mark where each missing enzyme blocks the cycle. Any block stops urea, so NH₃ rises and the excess is parked as glutamine (Gln) and alanine (Ala). The cycle makes arginine, so arginine falls, except in arginase (ARG) deficiency, where it piles up. Tell the defects apart by what builds up before the block. OTC (also called ornithine carbamoyltransferase): unused carbamoyl phosphate (CP) leaks out of the mitochondria into the cytosol, where ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase, pyrimidine pathway) turns it into orotic acid. CPS1: no CP, so no orotic acid. ASS: citrulline. ASL: argininosuccinate.

Normal plasma NH₃ is under about 35 µM; a newborn with a complete urea cycle defect is usually above 150 µM. NH₃ stimulates the brain's breathing center, so the baby breathes fast and blows off CO₂, causing respiratory alkalosis. The edema comes from glutamine swelling astrocytes. Partial defects stay silent until protein breakdown rises (illness, fasting, stress) and overwhelms the weak cycle.

Phenylbutyrate becomes phenylacetate, which joins glutamine; the product (phenylacetylglutamine) leaves in urine and carries 2 N out without the urea cycle. Citrulline (CPS1 or OTC deficiency) enters the cycle after the block and picks up aspartate's N. Arginine (ASS deficiency = citrullinemia; ASL deficiency = ASA, argininosuccinic aciduria) replaces the arginine the cycle can't make, regenerates ornithine and activates NAG synthase.

Both defects give the same top line: NH₃ up, glutamine up, BUN (blood urea nitrogen) down. Carbamoyl phosphate tells them apart. CPS-I deficiency (type 1): it cannot be made, so it is low. OTC deficiency (type 2): it is made but cannot join ornithine, so citrulline is low. The carbamoyl phosphate piles up and spills into pyrimidine synthesis, so orotic acid and uracil rise. Treatment cuts the nitrogen load: less dietary protein, plus benzoate (binds glycine) and phenylbutyrate (binds glutamine), whose products leave in urine.

Answer: A, ammonia. OTC (ornithine transcarbamoylase) joins carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine to make citrulline. Without it the cycle stops at step 2, so NH₃ is not removed and rises. Everything made after the block falls: citrulline, arginine and urea are all low. Citrulline is high only when the block comes after it (argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency). Tyrosine is not part of the urea cycle.
Answer: D. AST and ALT only transfer the amino group to α-KG to make glutamate; no free NH₃ is released. MAO, glutamate dehydrogenase, glutaminase and adenosine deaminase all release free NH₃.

Answer: D (OTC deficiency). High NH₃ + low BUN = urea is not being made; fast breathing = NH₃-driven respiratory alkalosis. Orotic acid points to OTC: carbamoyl phosphate is made but can't enter the cycle, so it spills into pyrimidine synthesis. CPS1 deficiency looks the same but has no orotic acid, because no carbamoyl phosphate is made.

qs.q: How does high NH₃ starve the brain of energy?
opts: It pulls α-ketoglutarate out of the TCA cycle
It blocks glucose entry into the brain
It speeds urea synthesis in neurons
qs.why: Excess NH₃ drives α-ketoglutarate → glutamate → glutamine, draining α-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate from the TCA cycle, so ATP production falls.

qs.q: In hyperammonemia, which brain cells store NH₃ as glutamine and swell, causing brain edema?
qs.why: Glutamine enters astrocyte mitochondria, where glutaminase frees NH₃ again; the resulting ROS damage the mitochondria and the astrocytes swell.

qs.q: Why does cirrhosis raise blood ammonia?
opts: Portal blood bypasses the liver, so less urea is made
qs.why: Collateral vessels shunt portal blood into the systemic circulation, so gut NH₃ never reaches the hepatocytes that turn it into urea.

qs.q: Which source contributes the most NH₃ to the blood?
qs.why: About 50% of blood NH₃ comes from the gut (mostly colon) and about 40% from the kidney; muscle and red cells add about 5% each.

qs.q: Which enzyme carries out oxidative deamination of glutamate in the liver and kidney?
qs.why: Glutamate dehydrogenase strips glutamate's amino group as NH₃ and gives back α-ketoglutarate. The aminotransferases only move amino groups and release no free NH₃.

qs.q: What is unusual about glutamate dehydrogenase's coenzyme use?
opts: It can use either NAD⁺ or NADP⁺
qs.why: Glutamate dehydrogenase uniquely uses both NAD(H) and NADP(H). Pyridoxal phosphate is the cofactor of aminotransferases, not of this enzyme.

qs.q: In the liver after a protein meal, which way does glutamate dehydrogenase run?
qs.why: In liver it releases NH₃ for urea and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) for the TCA cycle. The reverse, trapping NH₃ in glutamate with NADPH, happens when NH₃ is high, as in the brain.

qs.q: Which enzyme adds NH₃ to glutamate in muscle and brain so NH₃ can travel safely in blood?
qs.why: Glutamine synthetase (uses ATP) traps NH₃ as glutamine; glutaminase in liver, kidney and gut releases it again.

qs.q: Which amino acid is the most abundant free amino acid in blood?
qs.why: Glutamine (about 500 µM) makes up more than 20% of free amino acids in blood and 40% in muscle, because tissues make it to scavenge NH₃.

qs.q: In tumor glutaminolysis, which two enzymes each release one NH₃ from glutamine?
qs.why: Glutaminase turns glutamine into glutamate + NH₃; glutamate dehydrogenase turns glutamate into α-ketoglutarate + NH₃, which then enters the TCA cycle for energy.

qs.q: Which bacterial enzyme in the gut and stomach releases NH₃ from urea?
qs.why: Bacterial urease (including H. pylori in the stomach) splits urea into CO₂ and NH₃, which the portal vein carries to the liver. Arginase makes urea rather than breaking it down.

qs.q: Which enzyme releases NH₃ while breaking down catecholamines such as norepinephrine?
qs.why: Monoamine oxidase removes the amine group of dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine as NH₃.

qs.q: Why are monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors used as antidepressants?
opts: They lower ammonia levels in the brain
They block monoamine release from neurons
They speed the reuptake of monoamines
They block monoamine breakdown, raising transmitter levels
qs.why: Blocking MAO prevents the breakdown of monoamine neurotransmitters, so more of them are available.

qs.q: Which enzyme releases NH₄⁺ during purine breakdown?
qs.why: Adenosine deaminase removes the amino group of adenosine as NH₄⁺ during purine catabolism.

qs.q: Where do urea's two nitrogen atoms come from?
opts: Free NH₃ (as carbamoyl phosphate) and aspartate
qs.why: One N enters as NH₃ in carbamoyl phosphate; aspartate donates the second. Both trace back to glutamate, via glutamate dehydrogenase and AST.

qs.q: How many high-energy phosphate bonds are spent to make one urea?
qs.why: Three ATP are used, but one is split to AMP + PPi, which costs two high-energy bonds, so the total is four.

qs.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle?
qs.why: CPS I in the mitochondrial matrix makes carbamoyl phosphate from CO₂ + NH₃ using 2 ATP. CPS II is cytosolic, uses glutamine and starts pyrimidine synthesis.

qs.q: Which molecule is the required allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I?
qs.why: CPS I works only when N-acetylglutamate binds it. Arginine acts one step earlier, stimulating N-acetylglutamate synthase (acetyl-CoA + glutamate).

qs.q: Ornithine transcarbamoylase joins ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate to make what?
qs.why: The carbamoyl group, carrying the first N, moves onto ornithine in the mitochondrion; the citrulline formed is exported to the cytosol in exchange for ornithine.

qs.q: Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine into NO and which by-product?
qs.why: Arginine + NADPH + O₂ → NO + citrulline. Arginase, not NO synthase, splits arginine into ornithine and urea.

qs.q: Argininosuccinate lyase splits argininosuccinate into arginine and which molecule?
qs.why: Aspartate's N stays on arginine and its carbon skeleton leaves as fumarate, which links the urea cycle to the TCA cycle (fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate → aspartate).

qs.q: The kidney makes arginine from citrulline but cannot make urea. Which enzyme does it lack?
qs.why: The kidney has argininosuccinate synthetase and lyase, so it turns gut-made citrulline into arginine, but only the liver has arginase to split arginine into urea.

qs.q: Arginase splits arginine into urea and which molecule?
qs.why: Arginase, found only in the liver, releases urea and regenerates ornithine, which returns to the mitochondrion for the next turn of the cycle.

qs.q: Which two urea cycle enzymes act in the mitochondrial matrix?
opts: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamoylase
qs.why: Steps 1–2 (CPS I, OTC) are mitochondrial; steps 3–5 (argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, arginase) are cytosolic.

qs.q: Why can kidney failure raise blood ammonia?
opts: The failing kidney makes extra glutamine
More urea reaches the gut, where bacterial urease releases NH₃
Renal arginase releases NH₃ into blood
qs.why: High blood urea means more urea diffuses into the intestine; bacterial urease splits it into NH₃, and the portal vein carries it back to the liver.

qs.q: Which condition lowers BUN (blood urea nitrogen)?
qs.why: BUN falls when the liver makes less urea. Dehydration lowers filtration, and a high-protein diet or digested blood from a GI bleed adds amino acids, so all three raise BUN.

qs.q: Which state induces (increases) the urea cycle enzymes?
opts: The fed state with high insulin
qs.why: In fasting, glucagon drives gluconeogenesis from amino acids such as muscle alanine, and their amino groups must leave as urea. A high-protein diet induces the enzymes too.

qs.q: Which urea cycle disorder is the most common and X-linked?
qs.why: OTC deficiency is the most common (about 1:25,000) and the only X-linked one. CPS I deficiency is the most severe; argininosuccinate lyase deficiency is second most common.

qs.q: Why is urinary orotic acid high in ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiency but not in carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency?
opts: Unused carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis
Arginase releases orotic acid from arginine
Ammonia condenses directly into orotic acid
Excess citrulline is converted into orotic acid
qs.why: In OTC deficiency carbamoyl phosphate is made in the mitochondria but cannot enter the cycle, so it leaks out into the cytosol, where aspartate transcarbamoylase (pyrimidine pathway) turns it into orotic acid. Without CPS I, no carbamoyl phosphate is made.

qs.q: Why do newborns with a complete urea cycle defect develop respiratory alkalosis?
opts: Ammonia stimulates the breathing center, causing hyperventilation
Urea buffers H⁺ in the blood
The kidneys excrete extra H⁺ as NH₄⁺
qs.why: NH₃ stimulates the brain's respiratory center; the baby breathes fast, blows off CO₂, and blood pH rises.

qs.q: How does sodium phenylbutyrate lower blood ammonia?
opts: It activates carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
Its product phenylacetate joins glutamine for urinary excretion
It inhibits glutamine synthetase in muscle
It blocks bacterial urease in the gut
qs.why: Phenylbutyrate is a prodrug of phenylacetate, which combines with glutamine; phenylacetylglutamine leaves in urine, carrying 2 N out without the urea cycle.

qs.q: Which supplement is given in CPS I or OTC deficiency because it enters the cycle after the block?
qs.why: Citrulline enters past the CPS I and OTC steps and picks up aspartate's nitrogen, so the cycle can still remove some N. Glutamine and alanine would only add nitrogen.

qs.q: In which urea cycle disorder is arginine already high, so it is not supplemented?
qs.why: Every other urea cycle defect lowers arginine, so it must be replaced; in arginase deficiency arginine piles up (5–7× normal).

qs.q: A patient has high plasma NH₃ and a low BUN (blood urea nitrogen). What does this combination indicate?
opts: The liver is not making urea
The kidneys are not filtering urea
qs.why: Low BUN with high NH₃ means NH₃ is not being turned into urea, as in a urea cycle defect. Poor filtration, high protein intake or dehydration would raise BUN.

slides.note: Every amino acid splits into two parts. The amino group (red circle) comes off and leaves the body as urea. The carbon skeleton (blue box, now an α-keto acid) is burned for energy or becomes glucose or ketone bodies, depending on which molecule it turns into. TCA = tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle.

The triangle is the liver. Most tissues load waste nitrogen onto glutamine, which travels in the blood. In the liver, glutamine and glutamate release NH₃, which becomes urea; the kidney excretes the urea (the major exit). Intestinal cells split glutamine and send its NH₃ to the liver. The kidney proximal tubule cell secretes NH₃ into the tubule fluid (lumen), where it binds H⁺ and leaves in urine as NH₄⁺ (the minor exit; it also removes acid). Muscle sends alanine; the liver turns it into pyruvate → glucose, which returns to muscle. ALT, AST = aminotransferases.

Rule: a skeleton that becomes pyruvate or a TCA intermediate (red boxes) can make glucose, because all of these lead to oxaloacetate → phosphoenolpyruvate → glucose. A skeleton that becomes acetyl CoA or acetoacetate (blue box) can only make ketone bodies, because acetyl CoA cannot be turned back into pyruvate. Leucine and lysine give only acetyl CoA/acetoacetate. The three aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr, Trp) plus isoleucine give both.

DHAP = dihydroxyacetone phosphate; it interconverts with glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, and both can be built back up into glucose. In fasting, muscle protein breaks down and alanine carries its carbons to the liver, where it becomes pyruvate → glucose. Don't confuse: fatty acids normally cannot make glucose; only the last 3 carbons of an odd-chain fatty acid (propionyl CoA) can.

Answer: C. Pyruvate can be turned into oxaloacetate and then built up into glucose, so any amino acid whose carbon skeleton becomes pyruvate (alanine, serine, glycine, cysteine) is glucogenic. A ketogenic amino acid gives acetyl CoA or acetoacetate instead. Essential and non-essential describe whether the body can make the amino acid, not what its skeleton becomes.

Conditionally essential = normally made, but the supply can fall short. Tyrosine needs enough phenylalanine (and a working phenylalanine hydroxylase); cysteine needs enough methionine. Arginine is made via ornithine and the urea cycle, but not fast enough for a growing child.

Answer: E (arginine). The body makes its arginine with the urea cycle enzymes. When one of them is missing, too little arginine is made, so it becomes essential and must come from the diet. The one exception is arginase deficiency, the last step, where arginine builds up instead. The other four choices are non-essential and are still made normally.

Left picture, read downward (breakdown): asparaginase splits asparagine into aspartate + NH₃, and transamination turns aspartate into oxaloacetate. Synthesis runs upward: transamination is reversible, but asparagine is made by a different enzyme, asparagine synthetase (aspartate + an amide N from glutamine, using ATP). Right picture: the drug asparaginase destroys asparagine in the blood. Healthy cells make their own (check mark), but ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia) lymphoblasts lack asparagine synthetase (red X), so they cannot make protein and die.

Glutaminase removes glutamine's amide NH₂ as NH₃, leaving glutamate. Glutamate → α-KG (α-ketoglutarate) two ways: transamination (glutamate hands its amino group to a keto acid) or glutamate dehydrogenase (releases free NH₃). Both are reversible, so they also build glutamate. Right panels: a keto acid (blue) picks up an amino group and becomes its amino acid (red): pyruvate ⇄ alanine, OAA ⇄ aspartate, α-KG ⇄ glutamate. Glutamine is rebuilt by a different enzyme, glutamine synthetase (glutamate + NH₃ + ATP). PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, vitamin B6) is the cofactor of every aminotransferase.

Both lines are routes into α-KG. Arginine → ornithine (arginase) → glutamate semialdehyde → glutamate → α-KG; proline is also oxidized to glutamate. For synthesis, read the arrows right to left: glutamate → glutamate semialdehyde → proline, or → ornithine → urea cycle → arginine. So proline and arginine both come from glutamate, via glutamate semialdehyde. The kidney finishes arginine (from citrulline made in the gut) and releases it into the blood, because it lacks the liver's urea-cycle arginase that would split it into urea.

Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (PLP) moves one carbon between glycine and serine: glycine + a carbon from N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF (tetrahydrofolate, the active folate) → serine; the reverse (serine → glycine) hands the carbon back to THF. Serine itself is mainly made from 3-phosphoglycerate, a glycolysis intermediate. Serine dehydratase turns serine into pyruvate. In humans, threonine goes mainly to succinyl CoA (via propionyl CoA).

Answer: D. Arginine is made from glutamate via ornithine, but a growing child cannot make enough (conditionally essential). Tryptophan, threonine and phenylalanine are essential, so they cannot be made at all; serine is made freely from 3-phosphoglycerate.

BH₄ (tetrahydrobiopterin) is the cofactor of the three aromatic amino acid hydroxylases: Phe → Tyr, Tyr → DOPA (first step to catecholamines), Trp → 5-hydroxytryptophan (first step to serotonin). Nitric oxide synthase (Arg → NO) also needs it. Each reaction oxidizes BH₄ to BH₂ (dihydrobiopterin); dihydropteridine reductase rebuilds BH₄. The body makes BH₄ from GTP, so it is not a vitamin.

Dihydropteridine reductase (the ‘BH₂ reductase’) uses NADH or NADPH to turn BH₂ back into BH₄. Missing it, or missing a BH₄-making enzyme, leaves no BH₄. Phe then builds up, as in PKU (phenylketonuria), and dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin fall. That transmitter loss causes the neurologic signs, so a low-Phe diet alone does not fix it. Treat with BH₄ (sapropterin) plus L-DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan.

THB is another name for BH₄. A slash through THB means the cofactor is missing, so all three hydroxylases stop at once. Red arrows show blood levels: Phe rises and Tyr falls; dopamine, NE (norepinephrine) and E (epinephrine) fall; serotonin falls. This is non-classical PKU: Phe is high although PAH (phenylalanine hydroxylase) itself is normal. Treatment has to cover all three blocks: restrict Phe, give BH₄, and give DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan, the products just past the blocked steps.

Read the left column downward: the one carbon on THF gets more reduced at each step: formyl (–CHO) → methenyl (=CH–) → methylene (–CH₂–) → methyl (–CH₃). Each form has its job (blue boxes): N¹⁰-formyl → purines; N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene → dTMP (deoxythymidine monophosphate, the T of DNA) and serine; N⁵-methyl → methionine. MTHFR = methylene-THF reductase. The neural tube closes about 4 weeks after conception, often before pregnancy is known, so folate must be adequate beforehand.

Histidine breaks down via FIGLU (N-formiminoglutamate). The last step hands FIGLU's one-carbon group to THF, leaving glutamate → α-KG. With folate deficiency there is no THF to take it (red X), so FIGLU builds up (red arrows) and spills into urine, especially after a histidine load (the FIGLU test). Histidinemia is a different defect: missing histidase, the first step, so histidine itself rises in blood and urine.

Read the wide arrow downward. Met + ATP → SAM (S-adenosylmethionine). SAM gives its methyl to an acceptor → SAH (S-adenosylhomocysteine) → homocysteine. Homocysteine then has two exits. Remethylation (arrow turning right) back to Met by methionine synthase needs N⁵-methyl-THF (folate) and methyl-B12. Transsulfuration (arrow continuing down) needs vitamin B6: homocysteine + serine → cystathionine → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate (→ succinyl CoA). Low folate, B12 or B6 raises homocysteine, a vascular risk factor; missing cystathionine β-synthase causes homocystinuria.

Each target receives SAM's methyl group; SAM then becomes SAH → homocysteine, which is recycled to methionine. Polyamines are the exception: they take SAM's aminopropyl part, not its methyl. Methylation is needed to build and keep myelin, so poor methylation (e.g., low B12) can cause demyelination.

Homocysteine has two exits. Pathway 1, read downward: cystathionine synthase (cystathionine β-synthase), with pyridoxine (vitamin B6), turns it into cystathionine → cysteine. Pathway 2, read upward: methionine synthase, with methyl folate (N⁵-methyl-THF) and methylcobalamin (B12), turns it back into methionine. The slash shows pathway 1 blocked, which is classic homocystinuria. Red arrows are blood levels: homocysteine rises and cystathionine falls. The backed-up homocysteine is pushed through pathway 2, so methionine rises too.

Read from the bottom up. Methyl-THF hands its methyl group to cobalamin (vitamin B12), making methylcobalamin and freeing THF. Methylcobalamin then hands the methyl to homocysteine, making methionine. Without B12 (red X on cobalamin), methyl-THF cannot unload its methyl (small red cross). Folate gets stuck as methyl-THF (red up arrow) and no free THF comes back: the folate trap. The other folate jobs, such as making dTMP for DNA, then fail, so B12 deficiency causes the same megaloblastic anemia (large, immature red cells) as folate deficiency.

Answer: D. Very high homocysteine damages blood vessels and causes clots, so even a child can have a heart attack. Deficiency of cystathionine β-synthase (classic homocystinuria) blocks homocysteine → cystathionine. Homocysteine backs up and is remethylated, so methionine rises as well. A methionine synthase defect (E) also raises homocysteine, but methionine would be low, because it could not be remade.

All five feed propionyl CoA (mnemonic VOMIT, left to right: Val, Odd-chain fatty acids, Met, Ile, Thr). Propionyl CoA carboxylase (needs biotin) turns propionyl CoA into methylmalonyl CoA. Methylmalonyl CoA mutase (needs B12, in its adenosylcobalamin form) turns that into succinyl CoA, which can become glucose. Low B12 blocks the mutase, so methylmalonic acid rises; this separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency.

The red X marks a failed mutase step: either the enzyme itself is defective or its B12 coenzyme, adenosylcobalamin, is missing. Blue arrows show the result. Methylmalonyl CoA builds up (up arrow) and spills into the blood and urine as methylmalonic acid; succinyl CoA falls (down arrow), so these carbons cannot reach glucose. When the block is inherited (methylmalonic acidemia), the acid causes a metabolic acidosis in the first days of life.

Enzymes fall into six classes by the type of reaction. Find the three that matter here. Class 2: serine hydroxymethyltransferase is a transferase; it moves a one-carbon group from serine to THF. Class 5: methylmalonyl CoA mutase is an isomerase; it rearranges methylmalonyl CoA into succinyl CoA (a mutase is one kind of isomerase). Class 6: carboxylases that use ATP, such as pyruvate carboxylase and propionyl CoA carboxylase, are ligases. Dehydrogenases and hydroxylases are oxidoreductases (class 1); kinases are transferases.

Answer: D (isomerase). Methylmalonic acid is high, so methylmalonyl CoA cannot become succinyl CoA. That step belongs to methylmalonyl CoA mutase, an isomerase that needs B12 (adenosylcobalamin). The acid that builds up causes the metabolic acidosis with a large anion gap (an extra, unmeasured acid in the blood). The carboxylase (A) is one step earlier: if it failed, propionyl CoA would build up and methylmalonic acid would be low.

Vitamin B12 works in only two reactions, each with its own B12 form. (1) Methylmalonyl CoA mutase uses adenosylcobalamin to make succinyl CoA. (2) Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin: it moves a methyl from methyl folate (N⁵-methyl-THF) onto homocysteine to make methionine (read pathway 2 upward). So B12 deficiency raises both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine; folate deficiency raises only homocysteine. The carboxylase in pathway 1 needs biotin, not B12.

A recap of the carriers and their active forms. THF (tetrahydrofolate) carries one carbon in three forms: methyl-THF for remaking methionine, formyl-THF for purines, methylene-THF for dTMP and serine. Cobalamin (B12) has two forms: methylcobalamin for methionine synthase and adenosylcobalamin for methylmalonyl CoA mutase. SAM donates the methyl group in nearly every other methylation.

Tyrosine hydroxylase (needs BH₄, written H₄-biopterin) is the rate-limiting step. Dopamine β-oxidase is the same enzyme as dopamine β-hydroxylase (needs copper and vitamin C). The last step, norepinephrine (NE) → epinephrine, is PNMT (phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase), using a methyl from SAM. Cortisol from the adrenal cortex induces PNMT, so epinephrine is made mainly in the adrenal medulla. Side branch: in melanocytes, tyrosinase (a copper enzyme) makes melanin; no tyrosinase = albinism.

Two enzymes inactivate catecholamines, in either order: MAO (monoamine oxidase) removes the amine; COMT (catechol-O-methyltransferase) adds a methyl from SAM. Dopamine ends as HVA (homovanillic acid). Epinephrine and norepinephrine end as VMA (vanillylmandelic acid), either through metanephrine/normetanephrine (COMT first) or through dihydroxymandelic acid (MAO first). A pheochromocytoma (adrenal medulla tumor making catecholamines) raises urine VMA and metanephrines (red up arrows).

Tyrosine has two paths. Left, its precursor role: tyrosine hydroxylase, with THB (BH₄), starts the chain DOPA → dopamine → NE → E. Right, its breakdown: tyrosine → homogentisate → fumarylacetoacetate → fumarate + acetoacetate, which makes tyrosine both glucogenic and ketogenic. Each slash marks an inherited enzyme block, and the red up arrow marks what builds up. Without homogentisate oxidase, homogentisate builds up: alkaptonuria (urine turns black; dark pigment in cartilage, called ochronosis). Without fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, fumarylacetoacetate builds up: tyrosinemia type I.

Niacin (vitamin B3, used to build NAD⁺): too little causes pellagra, with dermatitis (the neck rash pictured), diarrhea and dementia. Melatonin is made from serotonin in the pineal gland and regulates sleep. Hartnup disease: the gut and kidney transporter for neutral amino acids is defective, so tryptophan is poorly absorbed and lost in urine → too little niacin → pellagra-like rash and neurologic signs.

Trp → 5-hydroxytryptophan (tryptophan hydroxylase, BH₄) → serotonin (decarboxylase, PLP). Left, top: a carcinoid tumor makes lots of serotonin, MAO turns it into 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), so urine 5-HIAA rises (the diagnostic test). Left, bottom (MAO crossed out): an MAO inhibitor blocks that step, so serotonin stays high and 5-HIAA falls. SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) raise synaptic serotonin by blocking its reuptake into the neuron.

Answer: C. MAO (monoamine oxidase) breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine. An MAO inhibitor blocks this breakdown (catabolism), so more transmitter stays in the nerve ending and reaches the synapse. It does not speed up synthesis, so D and E are wrong. Blocking serotonin reuptake, a different way to raise synaptic serotonin, is what SSRIs do.

Removing the amino group leaves an α-keto acid (the carbon skeleton). Removing the carboxyl group as CO₂ (decarboxylation, needs PLP) leaves a biogenic amine, such as histamine, serotonin, dopamine or GABA.

Both are single decarboxylations that need PLP (vitamin B6). Histamine acts on H1 receptors (allergy, inflammation; blocked by antihistamines) and on stomach H2 receptors (acid secretion; blocked by H2-blocker acid reducers). Glutamate decarboxylase turns the brain's main excitatory transmitter into its main inhibitory one, GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid).

In the endothelial cell, cNOS (constitutive nitric oxide synthase) makes NO from L-arginine (L-arg). NO diffuses into the smooth muscle cell, where it activates GC (guanylyl cyclase) to make cGMP from GTP, which relaxes the muscle. Glycine is every third residue of collagen (Gly-X-Y). Glycine also supplies C4, C5 and N7 of the purine ring (blue).

Glutathione (G-SH; Glu-Cys-Gly) is the cell's main antioxidant. Glutathione peroxidase (a selenium enzyme) uses 2 G-SH to turn H₂O₂ into water, leaving G-S-S-G; glutathione reductase rebuilds G-SH with NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway. The lower-left picture is heme, not bile acid: glycine + succinyl CoA → ALA (δ-aminolevulinic acid) by ALA synthase (PLP), the rate-limiting step. Lower right: bile acids are conjugated to glycine or taurine.

Creatine needs two organs. The kidney moves arginine's amidino group onto glycine → guanidinoacetate; the liver adds a methyl from SAM → creatine. Muscle stores it as creatine phosphate, a quick ATP reserve for the first minutes of hard exercise. Creatine and creatine phosphate slowly and spontaneously cyclize into creatinine (arrows at lower left) at a steady rate set by muscle mass. Creatinine is cleared by filtration, so blood creatinine rises when GFR (glomerular filtration rate) falls.

Read each row across: compound (left) ← the amino acids it is built from (right). The right column sits slightly higher than the left, so match the rows by order. The last row is clipped at the bottom: pyrimidines ← aspartate and glutamine.

Answer: B (tryptophan). Tryptophan hydroxylase (needs BH₄) makes 5-hydroxytryptophan, which is decarboxylated to serotonin. Tyrosine (made from phenylalanine) gives dopamine and norepinephrine; histidine gives histamine.

qs.q: Which two amino acids are purely ketogenic?
qs.why: Leucine and lysine break down only to acetyl CoA or acetoacetate. Phe, Tyr, Trp and Ile are both glucogenic and ketogenic; alanine and serine are glucogenic.

qs.q: Why can a carbon skeleton that becomes only acetyl CoA not be used to make glucose?
opts: Acetyl CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate
Acetyl CoA is converted directly into urea
Acetyl CoA is excreted unchanged in urine
Acetyl CoA cannot enter the TCA cycle
qs.why: Glucose needs pyruvate or a TCA intermediate that leads to oxaloacetate. The pyruvate → acetyl CoA step is one-way, so acetyl CoA can only form ketone bodies or be burned.

qs.q: Which part of fatty acid breakdown can be used to make glucose?
opts: Acetyl CoA from even-chain fatty acids
Malonyl CoA from fatty acid synthesis
Propionyl CoA from odd-chain fatty acids
qs.why: Fatty acids normally cannot make glucose; only the last 3 carbons of an odd-chain fatty acid (propionyl CoA → succinyl CoA) can.

qs.q: Which of these amino acids must normally come from the diet?
qs.why: Threonine is essential. Tyrosine is made from phenylalanine, serine from 3-phosphoglycerate and alanine from pyruvate.

qs.q: Tyrosine becomes essential when which enzyme is deficient?
qs.why: Tyrosine is made from phenylalanine by phenylalanine hydroxylase. Without it, tyrosine must come from the diet (conditionally essential).

qs.q: Why is asparaginase used to treat acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
opts: The leukemic cells lack asparagine synthetase
It releases ammonia that kills tumor cells
It converts asparagine into a toxic product
It blocks folate use by dividing cells
qs.why: Normal cells make their own asparagine, but these leukemic cells cannot, so they starve once asparaginase destroys blood asparagine.

qs.q: Glutamate becomes α-ketoglutarate either by transamination or by which enzyme that releases free NH₃?
qs.why: Glutamate dehydrogenase frees glutamate's amino group as NH₃. Glutaminase acts one step earlier, removing glutamine's amide N to give glutamate.

qs.q: Proline and arginine (via ornithine) are both made from which amino acid?
qs.why: Glutamate → glutamate semialdehyde, which leads either to proline or to ornithine and then arginine through the urea cycle.

qs.q: Serine is made mainly from which glycolytic intermediate?
qs.why: Serine comes mainly from 3-phosphoglycerate. Serine dehydratase later turns serine into pyruvate when it is broken down.

qs.q: When glycine is converted to serine, which cofactor supplies the extra carbon?
qs.why: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (a PLP enzyme) moves one carbon between glycine and serine, carried on N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF, the active folate.

qs.q: Tyrosine is broken down to fumarate and acetoacetate. What does that make it?
qs.why: Fumarate is a TCA intermediate that can become glucose; acetoacetate is a ketone body. So tyrosine (and phenylalanine) are both.

qs.q: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) is the cofactor for which enzymes?
qs.why: BH₄ serves the three aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and nitric oxide synthase. Aminotransferases and decarboxylases use pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).

qs.q: Why does a low-phenylalanine diet alone not fix BH₄ deficiency?
opts: Dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin synthesis still fails
Phenylalanine is made from tyrosine instead
BH₄ deficiency does not raise phenylalanine
BH₄ must come from the diet
qs.why: Without BH₄, tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases also fail, so neurotransmitters fall. Treatment adds BH₄ (sapropterin), L-DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan.

qs.q: Methotrexate competitively inhibits which enzyme?
qs.why: Methotrexate, a folate analogue, blocks dihydrofolate reductase, so folate cannot be reduced to active tetrahydrofolate. Dihydropteridine reductase regenerates BH₄, not folate.

qs.q: In folate deficiency, which compound rises in urine after a histidine load?
qs.why: Histidine breaks down to FIGLU, whose last step hands a one-carbon group to tetrahydrofolate (THF). Without enough folate there is no THF to take it, so FIGLU builds up and spills into urine.

qs.q: Homocysteine is remethylated to methionine using which two vitamins?
qs.why: Methionine synthase takes the methyl from N⁵-methyl-THF (folate) through methyl-B12. Vitamin B6 is needed for the other exit, transsulfuration to cysteine.

qs.q: Which amino acids are broken down to propionyl CoA?
qs.why: Mnemonic VOMIT: valine, odd-chain fatty acids, methionine, isoleucine and threonine all give propionyl CoA → methylmalonyl CoA → succinyl CoA → glucose.

qs.q: Which enzyme in the propionyl CoA pathway requires vitamin B12?
qs.why: Methylmalonyl CoA mutase needs B12; propionyl CoA carboxylase needs biotin. Low B12 raises methylmalonic acid, which separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency.

qs.q: Which conversion uses a methyl group donated by S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)?
qs.why: SAM methylates PE to PC (and NE to epinephrine, DNA and others). The other three are decarboxylations that need pyridoxal phosphate, not SAM.

qs.q: Which enzyme converts norepinephrine to epinephrine using a methyl group from SAM?
qs.why: PNMT adds SAM's methyl to norepinephrine; cortisol induces it, so epinephrine is made mainly in the adrenal medulla. COMT also uses SAM but inactivates catecholamines.

qs.q: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of catecholamine synthesis?
qs.why: Tyrosine hydroxylase (needs BH₄) turns tyrosine into DOPA and sets the pace. DOPA decarboxylase (PLP) and dopamine β-hydroxylase (copper, vitamin C) follow.

qs.q: Absence of tyrosinase causes which condition?
qs.why: In melanocytes, tyrosinase (a copper enzyme) starts the conversion of tyrosine to melanin; without it no melanin is made.

qs.q: A pheochromocytoma raises urinary levels of which catecholamine end product?
qs.why: MAO and COMT break epinephrine and norepinephrine down, in either order, to VMA, so a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medulla tumor raises urine VMA. Dopamine ends as homovanillic acid.

qs.q: Which compounds are made from tryptophan?
qs.why: Tryptophan gives niacin (vitamin B3) and serotonin; the pineal gland turns serotonin into melatonin. Dopamine, norepinephrine and melanin come from tyrosine.

qs.q: A carcinoid tumor raises urinary levels of which compound?
qs.why: A carcinoid tumor makes excess serotonin, which MAO converts to 5-HIAA, so urine 5-HIAA rises. VMA rises with pheochromocytoma.

qs.q: Removing an amino acid's carboxyl group as CO₂ produces what?
qs.why: Decarboxylation (needs PLP) leaves a biogenic amine such as histamine, serotonin, dopamine or GABA. Removing the amino group instead leaves an α-keto acid.

qs.q: Decarboxylating glutamate produces which neurotransmitter?
qs.why: Glutamate decarboxylase (PLP) turns the brain's main excitatory transmitter into its main inhibitory one, GABA. Histamine comes from decarboxylating histidine.

qs.q: Nitric oxide relaxes vascular smooth muscle by raising which second messenger?
qs.why: Endothelial NO synthase makes NO from arginine; NO diffuses into smooth muscle and activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP and causing relaxation.

qs.q: Glutathione, the cell's main antioxidant, is built from which amino acids?
qs.why: Glutathione is the tripeptide Glu-Cys-Gly; its cysteine -SH lets glutathione peroxidase turn H₂O₂ into water. Glycine, arginine and methionine build creatine.

qs.q: Heme synthesis starts by joining glycine with which molecule?
qs.why: ALA synthase (needs PLP) joins glycine and succinyl CoA into δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis.

qs.q: Why is serum creatinine used as a marker of GFR (glomerular filtration rate)?
opts: It rises after every protein-rich meal
It is fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
It forms at a steady rate and is cleared by filtration
The kidney makes it in proportion to GFR
qs.why: Creatine and creatine phosphate in muscle spontaneously cyclize to creatinine at a steady rate set by muscle mass, and the kidney clears it by filtration, so blood creatinine rises when GFR falls.
