lectures.title: Inborn Errors of Amino Acid Metabolism

slides.note: An aminoacidopathy is an inborn error of amino acid metabolism: one enzyme is missing, so an amino acid or a side product builds up. Each line ends on the scale at that disease's incidence per 100,000. Red stars mark the diseases to learn here.

Phe (phenylalanine) becomes Tyr (tyrosine) by PAH (phenylalanine hydroxylase), which needs O₂ and BH₄. In the reaction BH₄ turns into BH₂, which is recycled back to BH₄ with NADH. Each red bar marks a disease: a block at PAH or at BH₄ recycling causes PKU, at Tyr → melanin causes albinism, and in Tyr breakdown causes tyrosinemia. When PAH is blocked, Phe is turned instead into the side products at upper left (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate), which harm the brain.

Non-classical PKU comes from failure to make or recycle BH₄ (e.g. dihydropteridine reductase deficiency, the lower X). BH₄ is also the cofactor of tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, so these patients also lack dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin. A low-Phe diet alone does not fix their brain symptoms; they also need BH₄, L-DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan.

Hyperphenylalaninemia means high blood Phe from any cause. Left: PAH itself is defective (classical PKU), with almost no enzyme activity and Phe above 1 mM. Right: PAH is fine but its cofactor THB (another name for BH₄) is missing, because it is not made (synthesis) or not regenerated from BH₂ (recycling). Normal blood Phe is about 0.05 mM; 0.12 mM is the upper limit of normal.

Compare the panels: dark arrows are the main routes; faded arrows carry little. Normally Phe goes to Tyr. In PKU the block at phenylalanine hydroxylase sends Phe into phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate and phenylacetate, and less Tyr is left for its products (faded arrows), so less melanin is made and skin and hair are light (hypopigmentation).

With PAH blocked, Phe takes a minor route. An aminotransferase moves its amino group onto pyruvate (making alanine), using PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6). The product, phenylpyruvate, is a phenyl-ketone and gives the disease its name. It is turned into phenylacetate and phenyllactate; all three pass into the urine and give it a musty, “mousy” odor.

Blood Phe rises 20–50-fold. Phe shares one brain-entry transporter with the other large neutral amino acids (Tyr, Trp, Val, Leu, Ile) and wins the competition, so the brain runs short of them for protein, myelin and neurotransmitters. That is why treatment adds back Tyr, Trp and the branched-chain amino acids while restricting Phe. In PKU, Tyr becomes an essential amino acid.

A red arrow up means the substance rises; down means it falls. The black slash is the missing enzyme. Phe rises and harms the brain (CNS = central nervous system). The extra Phe spills into phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate and phenylacetate, which give the urine its musty odor. Tyr falls, so less melanin is made. Hence the treatment: less Phe, more Tyr. The cofactor cycle is normal here (THB = BH₄, DHB = BH₂).

A slash marks a step that fails without THB (BH₄). THB serves three hydroxylases, so three pathways fail together: Phe is not turned into Tyr (Phe rises); Tyr is not turned into DOPA, so dopamine, NE (norepinephrine) and E (epinephrine) fall; tryptophan is not turned into 5-OH-tryptophan (5-hydroxytryptophan), so serotonin falls. A low-Phe diet lowers Phe but does not bring back the neurotransmitters, so THB, DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan are given; the last two enter their pathways after the blocked step.
Answer: D. Classical PKU is a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase. Dihydropteridine reductase (A) deficiency causes the non-classical, BH₄-type PKU.

Answer: E. Seizures, lost milestones and a musty smell in an infant are untreated PKU. With phenylalanine hydroxylase blocked, Phe is turned into phenylpyruvate, then phenylacetate and phenyllactate, which cause the odor. Tetrahydrobiopterin (A) is the cofactor and does not build up. Succinylacetone (B) belongs to tyrosinemia type I and homogentisic acid (D) to alkaptonuria. Acetoacetate (C) is a normal end product of tyrosine breakdown.

Collect the clues. A baby who is well at first and then loses milestones after 3–4 months suggests a toxin that builds up slowly, as in an inborn error of metabolism. Fair skin and hair mean little melanin. A musty smell of body and urine is a classic odor clue. Birth in a remote town matters because newborn screening may never have been done.

A first seizure in an infant has many causes: infection, fever, head injury, a structural brain problem, a poison or a metabolic cause. Nothing in Pearl's story suggests infection, fever or injury. Her slow loss of milestones, odd smell and fair coloring point to the last line: an inborn error of metabolism.

Phe is 1300 µmol/L = 1.3 mM, about 26 times normal and above the 1 mM level of classical PKU. Is the enzyme or the cofactor at fault? Normal dihydropteridine reductase (measured in RBCs, red blood cells) means BH₄ recycling works. Normal urine BH₄ and BH₂ mean BH₄ synthesis works. So the fault is in PAH itself: classical PKU. (CBC = complete blood count; EEG = brain-wave recording.)

US newborns are all screened for PKU from a heel-prick blood spot, so the diet starts in the first days of life. Pearl was never screened, so Phe built up for 8 months. Tandem mass spectrometry measures many amino acids at once in that one spot. High Phe with low or low-normal Tyr points to PKU, because PAH makes Tyr from Phe. PAH is made in the liver, not in blood cells, so the enzyme cannot be tested in blood.

Each black box is one of Pearl's findings, placed on the step that explains it. (a) Fair skin and hair: little Tyr, so little melanin. (b) Lost and delayed milestones: high Phe blocks transport of other amino acids from blood into brain, so myelin and neurotransmitters fall. (c) Smell and musty urine: Phe spills into phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate and phenyllactate. (d) High serum Phe: PAH is blocked (red bar on the blue arrow). (e) Normal reductase, BH₄ and BH₂: the cofactor cycle is marked “normal”.

The diet is lifelong. All natural protein contains Phe, so most protein comes from a Phe-free formula; a little natural protein (for a baby, about 25% breast milk) supplies the Phe needed for growth. Aspartame is avoided because this sweetener contains Phe. Large neutral amino acids (aa) are added because high Phe blocks their entry into the brain. Sapropterin (Kuvan) is man-made BH₄ that boosts whatever PAH activity is left. Pegvaliase is an injected enzyme that breaks Phe down. Fish oil replaces the essential fatty acids (fa) that the diet lacks.

Left: an adult whose PKU was never treated, with severe intellectual disability. Right: PKU found by newborn screening and treated from the first days of life; development is normal. The diet must start in the first 7–10 days of life. Damage already done is largely permanent, so a diet started at 8 months, as for Pearl, prevents further harm but cannot fully undo the delay.

Tyrosine has two routes here. Left: tyrosine hydroxylase, which needs THB (BH₄), makes DOPA, then dopamine, NE (norepinephrine) and E (epinephrine). Right: tyrosine is broken down to fumarate and acetoacetate. A slash marks a missing enzyme; the red up arrow marks what builds up before it. No homogentisate oxidase: homogentisate builds up = alkaptonuria (black urine; ochronosis = dark pigment in cartilage). No fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase: fumarylacetoacetate builds up = tyrosinemia type I.

Read down the pathway; each disease (yellow) sits beside its blocked enzyme. THB = BH₄ (tetrahydrobiopterin) and DHB = BH₂ (dihydrobiopterin); dihydrobiopterin reductase is the same enzyme as dihydropteridine reductase. Nitisinone is a drug that blocks p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate oxidase. Ochronosis is the black pigment that alkaptonuria deposits in cartilage.

HT1 is a deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the last step. Fumarylacetoacetate and maleylacetoacetate back up and form succinylacetone, which damages the liver and the kidney tubules (the proximal tubule fails to reabsorb glucose, phosphate and amino acids, so they are lost in the urine) and blocks heme synthesis. Succinylacetone in blood or urine is the diagnostic marker. Nitisinone blocks an earlier step (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate oxidase, the upper bar) so these toxins never form; Tyr then rises, so the low-Phe/Tyr diet is still needed.

Both blocks sit before fumarylacetoacetate, so no succinylacetone forms and the liver is spared; instead tyrosine itself builds up. In HT2 (oculocutaneous tyrosinemia) Tyr is very high and forms crystals in the cornea and skin, causing the photophobia and painful palm/sole lesions. HT3 hits the same enzyme that nitisinone blocks.

Answer: A. Joint pain around age 40 with dark pigment in the whites of the eyes (sclerae) and the ear cartilage is alkaptonuria. Homogentisate oxidase, an enzyme of tyrosine breakdown, is missing. Homogentisic acid builds up and its dark polymer settles in cartilage (ochronosis), which damages the large joints. Phenylalanine (D) is tempting because Phe feeds into Tyr, but the block lies in tyrosine's own breakdown; a phenylalanine disorder means PKU.

Don't confuse tyrosinase (copper enzyme in melanocytes, no BH₄; Tyr → DOPA (dihydroxyphenylalanine) → melanin) with tyrosine hydroxylase (BH₄ enzyme in neurons and adrenal medulla; Tyr → DOPA → catecholamines). Without melanin the iris lets light through (red-looking eyes, photophobia) and the skin has no UV shield (skin cancer).
Answer: E. Succinylacetone forms from the backed-up fumarylacetoacetate (B) and maleylacetoacetate (D). It is the toxic product that damages liver and kidney, and the marker used to diagnose HT1.

Each branched-chain amino acid (BCAA: Val, Ile, Leu) first hands its amino group to α-ketoglutarate; then BCKD removes the carboxyl as CO₂ and adds CoA. BCKD works like PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase) and α-KGDH (α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) and shares their E3 subunit. Its cofactors come from vitamins: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) from B1, FAD from B2, NAD⁺ from B3, CoA from B5, plus lipoic acid. BCAA breakdown happens mainly in muscle, not liver.
Insulin turns on the BCKD gene. In type 2 diabetes the tissues respond poorly to insulin, so less BCKD is made and blood BCAAs (branched-chain amino acids) rise.

Answer: D. Thiamine becomes TPP, the cofactor of BCKD's E1 subunit; extra TPP can rescue a mutant E1 that binds it weakly. PDH, α-KGDH and transketolase also use TPP, but none of them is defective in MSUD. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses B12.

Methylmalonic acidemia and the homocysteine disorders both depend on these cofactors. THF (tetrahydrofolate, the active form of folate) carries a one-carbon group as methyl-, methylene- or formyl-THF. Cobalamin (vitamin B12) works in two forms, each for one enzyme: methyl-cobalamin for methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine), and adenosyl-cobalamin for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA). SAM (S-adenosylmethionine), made from methionine, hands its methyl group to other molecules.

Valine, isoleucine, methionine, threonine and odd-chain fatty acids all break down to propionyl-CoA. A carboxylase (needs biotin) turns it into methylmalonyl-CoA. Then methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, an isomerase that needs adenosyl-cobalamin (a B12 form), makes succinyl-CoA, which can go on to glucose. The red X means the mutase step fails. Blue arrows: methylmalonyl-CoA rises and leaves in the urine as methylmalonic acid; succinyl-CoA falls, so these carbons can no longer become glucose.

Propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA. The last step needs methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and its B12 form, adenosyl-cobalamin. Type I breaks either the enzyme (mut⁰ = no activity, mut⁻ = low) or the making of adenosyl-cobalamin (cblA, cblB). Methylmalonic acid builds up and causes acidosis. Backed-up propionyl-CoA blocks NAG (N-acetylglutamate) synthetase; without NAG, CPS-I (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first urea-cycle enzyme) stays off, so ammonia rises. Homocysteine stays normal, because the other B12 form, methyl-cobalamin, is still made.

Find row 5. An isomerase rearranges a molecule without adding or removing anything. The example is methylmalonyl-CoA mutase: one group (red) moves to the neighboring carbon, turning methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA. So a “mutase” is an isomerase. A carboxylase is a ligase (row 6): it joins CO₂ to a molecule using ATP. Dehydrogenases and hydroxylases are oxidoreductases (row 1); a kinase is a transferase (row 2).

Answer: D. High methylmalonic acid means methylmalonyl-CoA cannot be turned into succinyl-CoA. That step belongs to methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, an isomerase that needs adenosyl-cobalamin. The extra acid causes the acidosis with a large anion gap; glucose is low because these carbons no longer reach succinyl-CoA to be made into glucose. The carboxylase (A) is the step before; if it failed, methylmalonic acid would be low, not high.

Follow homocysteine (Hcy); it has two exits. (1) Back to methionine by methionine synthase, which needs methyl-cobalamin (B12) and takes the methyl from 5-methyl-TH₄ (TH₄ = tetrahydrofolate, active folate). (2) On to cysteine by cystathionine β-synthase, then cystathionase; both need PLP (B6). Around the cycle clockwise from the top: methionine + ATP makes SAM (S-adenosylmethionine), which gives its methyl to X (any molecule being methylated) and becomes S-adenosylhomocysteine, then Hcy. Low B6, B12 or folate lets Hcy build up.

Classic homocystinuria is cystathionine β-synthase deficiency: Hcy cannot go on to cysteine, so Hcy builds up and more of it is recycled to methionine; cysteine falls (it becomes essential). B12 or folate deficiency instead raises Hcy with normal or low methionine. The lens dislocates downward (in Marfan syndrome it goes upward), and blood clots are the main cause of early death. Some patients respond to large doses of B6.

Homocysteine has two exits, numbered 1 and 2; red arrows show what rises or falls in the blood. The slash blocks exit 1: cystathionine synthase (cystathionine β-synthase), whose coenzyme PLP comes from pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Homocysteine cannot become cystathionine, so homocysteine rises and cystathionine and cysteine fall. Exit 2 still works, so the extra homocysteine is turned back into methionine and methionine rises too. This pattern is classic homocystinuria.

Answer: D. A heart attack (myocardial infarction) in a child means severe early vessel damage and clotting, which very high homocysteine causes. Both homocysteine and methionine are raised, so the exit from homocysteine to cysteine is blocked (cystathionine synthase) and the backed-up homocysteine is recycled to methionine. Methionine synthase deficiency (E) also raises homocysteine, but methionine would be low, because homocysteine could not be turned back into it.

Methionine synthase passes one methyl group along a chain: from methyl-tetrahydrofolate to cobalamin (making methyl-cobalamin), then from methyl-cobalamin to homocysteine (making methionine). The red crosses show vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency: the chain stops. Homocysteine cannot become methionine, so homocysteine rises. Methyl-tetrahydrofolate cannot give its methyl away, so folate piles up in this one form (red up arrow) and too little free tetrahydrofolate is left for DNA synthesis. This is the methyl-folate trap.

These are the only two reactions in the body that need vitamin B12, each with its own form. (1) Methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA, by the mutase, uses adenosyl-cobalamin. (2) Homocysteine → methionine, by methionine synthase, uses methyl-cobalamin, and the methyl comes from methyl-folate. So too little B12 raises both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, while too little folate raises homocysteine only. Biotin, not B12, serves the carboxylase step.

Read from the top: B12 is processed down the middle (cblF, cblC, cblD; Cblₓ = cobalamin on its way to an active form), then splits. The left branch makes methyl-cobalamin for methionine synthase; the right branch (cblA, cblB) makes adenosyl-cobalamin for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. A block in the middle stops both branches, so labs show high methylmalonic acid and high homocysteine, the same pattern as dietary B12 deficiency. A cblA or cblB block stops only the right branch (type I). Folate deficiency raises homocysteine only.
Answer: C. Hcy inhibits lysyl oxidase, the copper enzyme that cross-links collagen fibers. Weakly cross-linked collagen makes a poor bone matrix, so bone mineral density falls.

qs.q: Besides O₂, which cofactor does phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) need to turn Phe into Tyr?
qs.why: PAH uses O₂ and BH₄; BH₄ is oxidized to BH₂ and recycled back with NADH. Copper belongs to tyrosinase, not PAH.

qs.q: Non-classical (secondary) PKU is caused by a defect in what?
qs.why: Classical PKU is PAH deficiency; non-classical PKU is failure to make or recycle BH₄ (for example, dihydropteridine reductase deficiency).

qs.q: Why does a low-Phe diet alone not fix the brain symptoms of BH₄-deficient PKU?
opts: BH₄ is also needed to make dopamine and serotonin
Tyr cannot cross into the brain
Blood Phe stays high despite the diet
BH₄ is needed to build myelin lipids
qs.why: BH₄ is also the cofactor of tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, so these patients also need BH₄, L-DOPA and 5-hydroxytryptophan.

qs.q: Why do people with classical PKU have light skin and hair?
opts: Too little Tyr is made for melanin
qs.why: PAH normally makes Tyr from Phe; with PAH blocked, Tyr is short and less melanin is made. Tyrosinase itself is normal and does not use BH₄.

qs.q: In PKU, how is phenylpyruvate formed from the excess Phe?
qs.why: An aminotransferase moves Phe's amino group onto pyruvate using PLP (vitamin B6), leaving the phenyl-ketone phenylpyruvate that spills into urine.

qs.q: Why does PKU treatment add Tyr, Trp and the branched-chain amino acids to the diet?
opts: High Phe blocks their entry into the brain
They speed Phe excretion in urine
qs.why: Phe shares one transporter (from blood into the brain) with the other large neutral amino acids and wins the competition. Tyr also becomes essential because it can no longer be made from Phe.

qs.q: To prevent maternal PKU syndrome, when must a woman with PKU start controlling her blood Phe?
opts: At the start of the second trimester
qs.why: High maternal Phe in early pregnancy causes fetal microcephaly, intellectual disability and heart defects, so control must start before conception and last through pregnancy.

qs.q: Hereditary tyrosinemia type I (HT1) is a deficiency of which enzyme?
qs.why: HT1 blocks the last step of Tyr breakdown, so fumarylacetoacetate backs up and forms toxic succinylacetone. Tyrosine aminotransferase is HT2; p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate oxidase is HT3.

qs.q: Nitisinone treats HT1 by inhibiting which enzyme?
qs.why: Blocking this step, upstream of the HT1 block, stops fumarylacetoacetate and succinylacetone from forming. Tyr then rises, so the low-Phe/Tyr diet is still needed.

qs.q: Photophobia plus painful lesions on the palms and soles point to which disorder?
qs.why: In HT2 (oculocutaneous tyrosinemia), very high Tyr forms crystals in the cornea and skin. HT3 instead causes intermittent ataxia.

qs.q: Why is the liver spared in tyrosinemia types II and III?
opts: The block is upstream, so no succinylacetone forms
Tyr is cleared quickly by the kidneys
Excess Tyr is diverted into melanin
The liver does not express these enzymes
qs.why: Both blocks sit before fumarylacetoacetate, so succinylacetone, the liver and kidney toxin of HT1, never forms; Tyr itself builds up instead.

qs.q: Alkaptonuria, with urine that turns brownish-black on standing in air, is a deficiency of which enzyme?
qs.why: Homogentisate builds up and spills into urine, where it auto-oxidizes in air and light and polymerizes into a dark pigment.

qs.q: What is the main disabling problem of alkaptonuria in adults?
qs.why: It is usually silent until about age 40; pigment deposits in cartilage (ochronosis) cause crippling arthritis, but the disease is not life-threatening.

qs.q: Tyrosinase, the melanin-making enzyme in melanocytes, uses which cofactor?
qs.why: Tyrosinase is a copper enzyme and does not need BH₄. Tyrosine hydroxylase, which makes catecholamines, is the BH₄ enzyme.

qs.q: Which step of branched-chain amino acid breakdown is defective in maple syrup urine disease (MSUD)?
opts: Oxidative decarboxylation of the keto acids
qs.why: MSUD is a deficiency of BCKD (branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase), which works like PDH. The first step, transamination, still works, so the keto acids pile up.

qs.q: Which amino acids are restricted in the diet in MSUD?
qs.why: These branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids build up and give urine the odor of burnt maple sugar.

qs.q: Which cofactor does methylmalonyl-CoA mutase need?
qs.why: The mutase turns methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA using adenosyl-cobalamin; type I MMA breaks the enzyme or the making of adenosyl-cobalamin (cblA, cblB).

qs.q: Why does methylmalonic acidemia cause hyperammonemia?
opts: Adenosyl-cobalamin is needed by the urea cycle
Propionyl-CoA blocks NAG synthetase, so CPS-I stays off
qs.why: Backed-up propionyl-CoA blocks N-acetylglutamate (NAG) synthetase; without NAG, CPS-I, the first urea-cycle enzyme, is inactive and ammonia rises.

qs.q: Methionine synthase turns homocysteine back into methionine using which cofactor?
qs.why: Methionine synthase takes a methyl group from 5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate (folate), passes it through methyl-cobalamin and puts it on homocysteine. Adenosyl-cobalamin serves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase instead.

qs.q: Cystathionine β-synthase, which sends homocysteine toward cysteine, needs which vitamin?
qs.why: Both cystathionine β-synthase and cystathionase use PLP. B12 and folate serve the other exit, back to methionine.

qs.q: In classic homocystinuria (cystathionine β-synthase deficiency), which amino acid becomes essential?
qs.why: Homocysteine cannot go on to cysteine, so homocysteine and methionine rise while cysteine falls and must come from the diet.

qs.q: Which lab result points to vitamin B12 deficiency rather than folate deficiency?
qs.why: B12 serves both methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase, so methylmalonic acid and homocysteine both rise; folate deficiency raises homocysteine only.

slides.note: SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) donates methyl groups; PAPS (3′-phosphoadenosine-5′-phosphosulfate) donates sulfate groups. UDP-glucose (uridine diphosphate-glucose) builds glycogen, and CDP-linked head groups (cytidine diphosphate) build phospholipids. Each of these carriers contains a nucleotide.

The ring is built step by step on PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate, the activated form of ribose 5-phosphate). The yellow numbers give the order in which atoms are added. Atoms per donor: glycine 3 (2 C + 1 N), glutamine 2 N, N¹⁰-formyl-THF 2 C, aspartate 1 N, CO₂ 1 C. THF = tetrahydrofolate, the form of folate that carries one-carbon units.

PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate, an activated ribose) gets its first nitrogen from glutamine in the committed step, glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase. AMP, IMP and GMP feed back to inhibit that step (the ⊖, left); the allopurinol and 6-mercaptopurine nucleotides (right) also inhibit it. Nine more steps build the ring on the sugar to make IMP (inosine monophosphate; base = hypoxanthine). IMP then branches: N from aspartate gives AMP; IMP dehydrogenase plus N from glutamine gives GMP.

The amidotransferase step (PRPP → 5-phosphoribosylamine) commits PRPP to purines, because 5-phosphoribosylamine has no other use. (PRPP synthetase is not committed: PRPP also feeds pyrimidine synthesis and salvage.) The end products AMP, GMP and IMP inhibit it; PRPP activates it. The drugs 6-mercaptopurine and allopurinol are turned into nucleotides by HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, a salvage enzyme), and those nucleotides also block this step.

Dotted lines are feedback: a red octagon means the enzyme is inhibited, the green circle means activated (PRPP activates the amidotransferase). Each product blocks the first enzyme of its own branch: AMP blocks adenylosuccinate synthetase, GMP blocks IMP dehydrogenase. The crossing solid lines show the balance: making AMP uses GTP, and making GMP uses ATP, so a surplus of one purine drives production of the other. When both are plentiful, they also shut off the amidotransferase and PRPP synthetase.

Mycophenolic acid blocks IMP dehydrogenase (IMP → XMP → GMP). B and T lymphocytes depend on de novo purine synthesis because they salvage poorly, so they run short of GMP and dGTP (deoxyguanosine triphosphate, a DNA building block) and cannot multiply. Most other cells keep going on salvage, so the drug mainly suppresses the immune attack on a transplant.
Answer: C, glycine. It donates 3 ring atoms (2 C + 1 N), more than any other source.

Phosphoribosylation = moving the ribose 5-phosphate from PRPP onto a free base, which releases pyrophosphate (PPi). Breakdown of the PPi makes the reaction irreversible. HGPRT salvages hypoxanthine (→ IMP) and guanine (→ GMP); APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase) salvages adenine (→ AMP). The black bars mark the two HGPRT steps that fail in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Salvage matters most in the brain.

Severity follows how much HGPRT activity is left: almost none → Lesch-Nyhan (neurologic signs, self-biting); partial → Kelley-Seegmiller (gout and uric acid kidney stones, no self-injury). In APRT deficiency, adenine cannot be salvaged and is oxidized to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which is insoluble and forms kidney stones (renal lithiasis).

Why uric acid rises: hypoxanthine and guanine that cannot be salvaged are broken down to uric acid. Also, the PRPP that HGPRT would have used builds up, while IMP and GMP fall. The amidotransferase gets more activator and less inhibition, so de novo synthesis speeds up and makes still more purine to degrade → hyperuricemia, gout and uric acid kidney stones. X-linked recessive, so it affects boys.
Self-mutilation in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: bitten lips (left) and a fingertip lost to biting (red circle).
Answer: A. HGPRT attaches guanine (and hypoxanthine) to PRPP. B, C and D are de novo steps and E is PRPP synthetase; all of these still work, and de novo synthesis actually speeds up.

CPS II (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II) makes carbamoyl phosphate from glutamine's amide N, CO₂ and 2 ATP. ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase) then adds aspartate. Pink ring atoms come from carbamoyl phosphate (C2, N3); blue atoms come from aspartate (N1, C4–C6). Only after the ring is closed does it receive ribose-phosphate from PRPP. UMP (uridine monophosphate) comes first; UTP (uridine triphosphate) → CTP (cytidine triphosphate) feeds RNA. The DNA thymine nucleotide, dTMP (labeled TMP), is made from dUMP (deoxyuridine monophosphate), not directly from UTP.

Follow the steps (left to right along the top, down the right side, then right to left along the bottom):
1. CPS II: glutamine + CO₂ + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate (the regulated step; see the regulation box).
2. ATCase adds aspartate → carbamoyl aspartate.
3. Dihydroorotase closes the ring → dihydroorotate.
4. Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (inner mitochondrial membrane) oxidizes it → orotate.
5. Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase adds ribose-P from PRPP → OMP (orotidine monophosphate).
6. OMP decarboxylase removes CO₂ → UMP.

Steps 1–3 are one cytosolic protein, CAD; steps 5–6 are one protein, UMP synthase, whose defect causes orotic aciduria.

Dotted lines are feedback: blue ⊖ = inhibits, red ⊕ = activates. UTP inhibits CPS II (long blue line on the left); ATP and PRPP activate it. UMP inhibits UMP synthase (OMP → UMP), and CTP inhibits CTP synthase (UTP → CTP). HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate) is the CO₂ source for carbamoyl phosphate.
Answer: A, aspartate (4 atoms: 3 C + 1 N). Glycine and N¹⁰-formyl-THF give none, because they donate only to purines.

Pyrimidine salvage goes through nucleosides: a phosphorylase adds the sugar (from ribose 1-phosphate) to the base, then a kinase adds the phosphate. Purine salvage is different: HGPRT and APRT attach ribose-phosphate from PRPP directly. Salvaged uridine bypasses the de novo pathway, which is why uridine treats orotic aciduria.

Hereditary orotic aciduria is a defect of UMP synthase, which does the last two steps (bottom row, right to left): orotate + PRPP → OMP, then OMP → UMP + CO₂. Orotate cannot become UMP, so it builds up and is lost in the urine. Less UMP means less UTP, so CPS II loses its feedback inhibition and makes even more orotate. Without pyrimidines, marrow cells cannot copy DNA → megaloblastic anemia (not fixed by B12 or folate), leukopenia and poor growth. Uridine is salvaged straight to UMP, past the block, and its UTP turns CPS II back down.

The wavy lines are the mitochondrial membrane: the upper-left area is inside the mitochondrion; everything else is cytosol. Follow the dashed line: with OTC (ornithine transcarbamoylase) blocked, carbamoyl phosphate made by CPS I in mitochondria leaks into the cytosol. It enters the pyrimidine path after CPS II, so UTP feedback cannot stop it, and orotate is made faster than UMP synthase can use it (OPT = orotate phosphoribosyltransferase, the first half of UMP synthase). Ammonia rises because the urea cycle is blocked, but pyrimidine supply stays normal, so there is no anemia.

N-glycosidic bond = the bond that joins the base to the sugar. Purines make it first (ring built on PRPP); pyrimidines make it last. In humans the regulated, rate-limiting step of pyrimidine synthesis is CPS II (inhibited by UTP); ATCase is the regulated step only in bacteria. The one mitochondrial enzyme is dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
Answer: B. UTP inhibits CPS II, the enzyme that produces carbamoyl phosphate. The others: A = PRPP synthetase, C = orotate phosphoribosyltransferase, D = dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, E = ATCase.

Ribonucleotide reductase replaces the 2′-OH of the ribose with H in ADP, GDP, CDP and UDP (one enzyme for all four). The hydrogens come from NADPH, passed through thioredoxin (recycled by thioredoxin reductase). dATP (deoxyadenosine triphosphate) turns the whole enzyme off and ATP turns it on, so too much dATP halts DNA synthesis. Hydroxyurea blocks this enzyme and starves dividing cells of DNA building blocks.

Follow the loop: thymidylate synthase uses N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF to add a methyl to dUMP → dTMP; the folate is left as DHF (dihydrofolate). DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase, uses NADPH) turns DHF back into THF, and THF picks up a new one-carbon unit to become methylene-THF again (left arrow). Methotrexate blocks DHFR, so THF runs out → no dTMP and no purines (which need N¹⁰-formyl-THF). 5-FU (5-fluorouracil), as its nucleotide 5-FdUMP (fluoro-dUMP), blocks thymidylate synthase itself.

Selectivity: humans don't make folate, so sulfonamides (which block folate synthesis) hit only microbes. Trimethoprim binds bacterial DHFR, and pyrimethamine binds protozoal DHFR, far more tightly than human DHFR. Methotrexate blocks human DHFR, so it is an anticancer drug. Bacteriostatic = stops growth without killing.
Compare the two ring structures: sulfanilamide looks like PABA (p-aminobenzoic acid, a building block of folate), so it competes with PABA at dihydropteroate synthetase.
Methotrexate looks almost like folate (NH₂ instead of OH at C4, a methyl on N10), so it binds DHFR very tightly. DHFR does both reductions shown (folate → DHF → THF), so both are blocked.

Normally thymidylate synthase grips dUMP through an enzyme cysteine (–SH), links it to methylene-THF, then pulls off the hydrogen at C5 to release dTMP. In 5-FdUMP, fluorine sits where that hydrogen must leave and cannot be removed, so enzyme, drug and folate stay locked in a stable covalent adduct. Suicide inhibitor = the enzyme's own reaction traps it.

All three are inactive until cells turn them into nucleotides. 6-MP (6-mercaptopurine) is activated by HGPRT; its nucleotide blocks IMP → AMP/GMP and the amidotransferase. 5-FU becomes F-UTP (built into RNA) and F-dUMP (blocks thymidylate synthase). AraC (cytosine arabinoside) carries arabinose instead of ribose; as araCTP it blocks DNA polymerase.

Correction: AZT is 3′-azido-3′-deoxythymidine, not 2′. Both drugs must be phosphorylated to nucleotides before they work. Neither has a 3′-OH, so once built into DNA, no next nucleotide can attach (chain termination). The herpes virus's own thymidine kinase does the first phosphorylation of acyclovir, so the active drug forms mainly in infected cells.
Answer: B, pyrimethamine. It blocks the DHFR of protozoa. Sulfonamides and trimethoprim target bacteria; methotrexate and 5-FU target human cells (anticancer).
Correction: AZT (zidovudine) is 3′-azido-3′-deoxythymidine, not 2′-azido. The azido group replaces the 3′-OH, which is why it stops DNA chain growth. Acycloguanosine = acyclovir.

qs.q: Which nucleotide-containing carrier donates methyl groups?
qs.why: SAM carries methyl groups; PAPS carries sulfate. UDP-glucose builds glycogen and CDP carriers build phospholipids.

qs.q: How does the salvage pathway make nucleotides?
opts: Builds rings from amino acids and CO₂
Breaks RNA down into new deoxynucleotides
Puts recovered bases back onto sugar phosphates
qs.why: Salvage reuses preformed bases and is economical; de novo synthesis builds rings from small building blocks and costs much more energy.

qs.q: Where is de novo purine synthesis most active?
qs.why: Other tissues have limited de novo purine synthesis and rely on salvage, partly of bases made in the liver; pyrimidine synthesis occurs in many tissues.

qs.q: Which folate carrier supplies carbon atoms to the purine ring?
qs.why: N¹⁰-formyl-THF donates 2 ring carbons; the other carbon donors are glycine and CO₂.

qs.q: Which nucleotide is the first complete purine and the branch point to AMP and GMP?
qs.why: The ring is built on PRPP to make IMP (base = hypoxanthine). IMP then branches: N from aspartate gives AMP; IMP dehydrogenase plus N from glutamine gives GMP.

qs.q: Ribose 5-phosphate used to make PRPP comes from which pathway?
qs.why: The HMP shunt makes ribose 5-phosphate, which PRPP synthetase activates to PRPP for both de novo and salvage synthesis.

qs.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of de novo purine synthesis?
qs.why: It makes 5-phosphoribosylamine, which has no other use. PRPP synthetase is not committed because PRPP also feeds pyrimidine synthesis and salvage.

qs.q: AMP feedback-inhibits which enzyme at the start of its own branch?
qs.why: Each product blocks the first enzyme of its own branch: AMP blocks adenylosuccinate synthetase, GMP blocks IMP dehydrogenase.

qs.q: Which nucleotide supplies the energy to convert IMP into AMP?
qs.why: Making AMP uses GTP and making GMP uses ATP, so a surplus of one purine drives production of the other.

qs.q: Mycophenolic acid prevents graft rejection by blocking which enzyme?
qs.why: B and T cells depend on de novo purine synthesis, so blocking IMP → GMP leaves them short of GMP and dGTP and they cannot multiply.

qs.q: What separates Lesch-Nyhan syndrome from Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome?
opts: How much HGPRT activity is left
qs.why: Both are HGPRT defects with high uric acid: under 1.5% activity gives Lesch-Nyhan (self-biting, neurologic signs); over 8% gives Kelley-Seegmiller (gout, kidney damage, no self-injury).

qs.q: Why does de novo purine synthesis speed up in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
opts: PRPP builds up while IMP and GMP fall
qs.why: The amidotransferase gets more activator (PRPP) and less feedback inhibition (IMP, GMP), so it makes extra purines that are degraded to uric acid.

qs.q: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) deficiency causes kidney stones of which compound?
qs.why: Adenine that cannot be salvaged is oxidized to insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which forms stones (renal lithiasis).

qs.q: How is Lesch-Nyhan syndrome inherited?
qs.why: The HGPRT gene is on the X chromosome and the disease is recessive, so it affects boys.

qs.q: Which three molecules supply the atoms of the pyrimidine ring?
qs.why: Carbamoyl phosphate (from glutamine's amide N and CO₂) joins aspartate to make the ring. Glycine and formyl-THF donate only to purines.

qs.q: Which enzyme of de novo pyrimidine synthesis is not cytosolic?
qs.why: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and oxidizes dihydroorotate to orotate; all the other enzymes are in the cytosol.

qs.q: UMP synthase carries which two enzyme activities?
qs.why: UMP synthase adds ribose-P from PRPP to orotate (making OMP) and then removes CO₂ to make UMP. CAD holds the first three activities (CPS II, ATCase, dihydroorotase).

qs.q: How does CPS II differ from CPS I?
qs.why: CPS II (pyrimidine synthesis) is cytosolic, takes N from glutamine, is inhibited by UTP and activated by ATP and PRPP. CPS I (urea cycle) is mitochondrial, uses ammonia, and needs N-acetylglutamate.

qs.q: CTP synthetase makes CTP by adding an amino group from glutamine to which nucleotide?
qs.why: UMP is phosphorylated to UDP and then UTP; CTP synthetase then aminates UTP, so cytidine nucleotides form at the triphosphate level.

qs.q: Which molecules activate CPS II?
qs.why: ATP and PRPP activate CPS II, and UTP inhibits it. N-acetylglutamate activates CPS I of the urea cycle.

qs.q: In pyrimidine salvage, which enzyme turns a free base into its nucleoside?
qs.why: The phosphorylase adds the sugar from ribose 1-phosphate, then a kinase adds phosphate. Purine salvage instead uses HGPRT and APRT to transfer ribose-P from PRPP.

qs.q: Hereditary orotic aciduria is a deficiency of which enzyme?
qs.why: Orotate cannot become UMP. Less UTP also means less feedback inhibition of CPS II, so even more orotate is made and spills into urine.

qs.q: Why does uridine treat hereditary orotic aciduria?
opts: It reactivates the defective UMP synthase
It is salvaged to UMP past the block
It speeds orotate excretion in urine
It supplies PRPP for OMP formation
qs.why: Salvaged uridine bypasses UMP synthase, and the UTP made from it turns CPS II back down.

qs.q: Which finding points to OTC deficiency, not UMP synthase deficiency, as the cause of orotic aciduria?
qs.why: OTC (ornithine transcarbamoylase) deficiency blocks the urea cycle, so ammonia rises and leaked carbamoyl phosphate makes orotate. Pyrimidine supply stays normal, so no anemia or leukopenia.

qs.q: In humans, which enzyme is the regulated, rate-limiting step of pyrimidine synthesis?
qs.why: CPS II is inhibited by UTP and activated by ATP and PRPP. Aspartate transcarbamoylase is the regulated step only in bacteria.

qs.q: In pyrimidine synthesis, when is the base joined to ribose 5-phosphate?
qs.why: Pyrimidines close the ring (orotate) first, then take ribose-P from PRPP. Purines do the reverse: the ring is built on PRPP from the start.

qs.q: dTMP (deoxythymidine monophosphate) is made from which nucleotide?
qs.why: Thymidylate synthase adds a methyl to dUMP to make dTMP; UTP feeds RNA and CTP synthesis instead.

qs.q: Ribonucleotide reductase makes deoxyribonucleotides at which phosphate level?
qs.why: One enzyme replaces the 2′-OH of ADP, GDP, CDP and UDP with H, using electrons from NADPH passed through thioredoxin.

qs.q: What is the major negative regulator of ribonucleotide reductase?
qs.why: dATP turns the whole enzyme off and ATP turns it on, so excess dATP halts DNA synthesis.

qs.q: Hydroxyurea fights cancer by inhibiting which enzyme?
qs.why: Blocking ribonucleotide reductase starves dividing cells of deoxyribonucleotides for DNA.

qs.q: At which phosphate level are cytidine nucleotides formed?
qs.why: CTP is made from UTP. Deoxyribonucleotides form at the diphosphate level and dTMP at the monophosphate level.

qs.q: Methotrexate inhibits which enzyme?
qs.why: Methotrexate looks almost like folate and binds human DHFR very tightly, blocking both folate → DHF and DHF → THF.

qs.q: Why does methotrexate stop purine synthesis as well as dTMP synthesis?
opts: THF runs out, so no N¹⁰-formyl-THF
qs.why: Purine synthesis needs N¹⁰-formyl-THF and dTMP synthesis needs N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene-THF; both come from THF, which DHFR regenerates.

qs.q: Why do sulfonamides not harm human cells?
opts: Humans take in folate rather than make it
Human DHFR does not bind them
qs.why: Sulfonamides mimic PABA and block dihydropteroate synthetase (folate synthase), which only microbes use to make folate.

qs.q: Trimethoprim inhibits which enzyme?
qs.why: Trimethoprim binds bacterial DHFR far more tightly than human DHFR. Pyrimethamine targets protozoal DHFR; methotrexate targets human DHFR.

qs.q: 5-Fluorouracil, as 5-FdUMP, inhibits which enzyme?
qs.why: 5-FdUMP blocks dUMP → dTMP. 5-FU also becomes F-UTP, which is built into RNA and disrupts RNA processing.

qs.q: Why is 5-FdUMP called a suicide inhibitor?
opts: The enzyme's own reaction traps it covalently
qs.why: Fluorine sits where the C5 hydrogen must leave; it cannot be removed, so enzyme, drug and methylene-THF stay locked in a stable covalent adduct.

qs.q: Which enzyme activates 6-mercaptopurine into its nucleotide?
qs.why: HGPRT turns 6-MP into a nucleotide that blocks IMP → AMP/GMP and the amidotransferase.

qs.q: Cytosine arabinoside (araC), as araCTP, inhibits what?
qs.why: AraC carries arabinose instead of ribose; once phosphorylated it blocks DNA polymerase and is used for leukemias and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

qs.q: Why do acyclovir and AZT stop DNA chain growth?
qs.why: Once built into DNA, no next nucleotide can attach without a 3′-OH. In AZT (3′-azido-3′-deoxythymidine) the azido group replaces the 3′-OH.

qs.q: Why is acyclovir activated mainly in herpes-infected cells?
opts: Viral thymidine kinase does its first phosphorylation
Viral DNA polymerase removes a blocking group
Only infected cells take up nucleosides
qs.why: The herpes virus's own thymidine kinase phosphorylates acyclovir first, so the active nucleotide forms mostly in infected cells.

qs.q: AZT (zidovudine) treats HIV by inhibiting which enzyme?
qs.why: Phosphorylated AZT blocks HIV reverse transcriptase and terminates the growing DNA chain.

slides.note: Every purine nucleotide follows the same steps: nucleotide → nucleoside (5′-nucleotidase removes the phosphate) → free base (PNP, purine nucleoside phosphorylase, removes the ribose) → xanthine → uric acid. Adenine first loses its amino group (AMP → IMP by AMP deaminase, or adenosine → inosine by ADA, adenosine deaminase), so it ends up as hypoxanthine. Guanine is deaminated to xanthine by guanine deaminase (guanase). Colored boxes mark the three key enzymes: ADA (green), PNP (red), xanthine oxidase (purple). IMP = inosine monophosphate (base: hypoxanthine); XMP = xanthosine monophosphate.

Xanthine oxidase does the last two steps: hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid. Each step uses O₂ and releases H₂O₂ (hydrogen peroxide). Its key metal cofactor is molybdenum; FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) and Fe-S (iron-sulfur) centers carry the electrons. Tissues outside the liver and gut have little of it, so their free bases are kept for salvage.

Answer: A. Xanthine oxidase oxidizes hypoxanthine → xanthine, then xanthine → uric acid. D (inosine → hypoxanthine) is PNP's reaction, E (adenosine → inosine) is ADA's, C skips the xanthine step, and B runs backward.

HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) and APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase) reattach free bases to ribose phosphate taken from PRPP, remaking IMP, GMP and AMP. This salvage pathway rescues about 90% of bases. The green and purple boxes mark the two bases HGPRT rescues. Without HGPRT, hypoxanthine and guanine can only be broken down (through xanthine, by xanthine oxidase) to uric acid, so uric acid rises.

PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate) is the activated ribose-phosphate donor for both salvage and new (de novo) purine synthesis. Salvage uses up PRPP and makes AMP, IMP and GMP, which inhibit glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase, the committed step of de novo synthesis. The black bars mark the HGPRT steps lost in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. So active salvage slows de novo synthesis; lost salvage (Lesch-Nyhan) speeds it up.

Underexcretion (the kidneys excreting too little urate) causes over 90% of hyperuricemia. Lactate raises urate through URAT1 (urate transporter 1) in the proximal tubule: it moves urate out of the tubular fluid into the tubule cell (reabsorption, so urate is kept) in exchange for lactate, which moves the other way, into the tubular fluid. More lactate means more urate reabsorbed and less excreted. Chemotherapy kills many cells at once and releases their purines, so uric acid spikes.

Under polarized light, gout crystals (MSU, monosodium urate) are needles, negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis). Pseudogout crystals (calcium pyrophosphate) are rhomboid, positively birefringent (blue when parallel). Tophi = chalky lumps of urate crystals in soft tissue; podagra = a gout attack in the big-toe (first metatarsophalangeal) joint.

HGPRT is almost absent, so hypoxanthine and guanine are not salvaged and become uric acid. Unused PRPP piles up and IMP/GMP fall, so de novo synthesis speeds up — a second source of urate. Orange "sand" in the diaper = uric acid crystals. Neurological signs include chorea and athetosis (jerky and writhing involuntary movements). Allopurinol lowers urate but does not fix the neurological or self-injury symptoms.

• von Gierke (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency): glucose 6-phosphate builds up and spills into the HMP shunt (hexose monophosphate shunt = pentose phosphate pathway) → more ribose 5-phosphate → more PRPP → more purines made and degraded. It also causes lactic acidosis, which cuts urate excretion.
  • Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency): fructose 1-phosphate traps phosphate, ATP can't be regenerated, and the extra AMP is broken down to urate.
  • Alcohol raises lactate, which blocks urate excretion.

Answer: D. More PRPP drives more de novo purine synthesis, and the extra purines are degraded to uric acid. B (more salvage), C (less xanthine oxidation, like allopurinol) and E (less AMP breakdown) all lower uric acid. A involves pyrimidines, which never become uric acid.

Each treatment targets one source; a red X marks where it acts. (2) A low-purine diet cuts intake (diet supplies about one-third of purines). (3) Xanthine oxidase inhibitors cut production in overproducers. (4) Uricosuric drugs raise kidney excretion in underexcretors (reduced renal clearance, blue X, is the most common cause). (1) NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), colchicine and steroids only calm the acute flare; they do not lower uric acid.

Colchicine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly, so neutrophils cannot move into the joint or engulf crystals. NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen, indomethacin) and steroids block the inflammatory products themselves. All three treat the acute attack only — uric acid does not change.

Allopurinol is a hypoxanthine look-alike. Xanthine oxidase converts it to oxypurinol, which stays tightly bound to the enzyme. In the double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot (x-axis = 1/[xanthine], y-axis = 1/V, V = reaction speed), the inhibited line is steeper but meets the y-axis at the same point: same Vmax (top speed), higher Km (more substrate needed) — the pattern of a competitive inhibitor. The hypoxanthine that builds up can be salvaged or excreted.

Tubule lumen (urine side, apical membrane) is on the right; blood side (basolateral membrane) is on the left. URAT1, in the apical membrane of the proximal tubule, moves urate out of the tubular fluid into the cell; urate then exits into the blood (arrows pointing left). This is reabsorption: urate is kept. In exchange, lactate or another organic anion moves from the cell into the tubular fluid. Probenecid and the listed drugs block URAT1 (‖), so more urate stays in the urine; they need working kidneys. More lactate drives more exchange, so alcohol and lactic acidosis raise blood urate.

Answer: C. An acute attack needs an anti-inflammatory drug. Naproxen (an NSAID) is the trap: NSAIDs worsen gastric ulcers. Probenecid, allopurinol and febuxostat lower uric acid over weeks and do not stop an acute flare.

One pathway, three diseases. ADA deficiency blocks adenosine → inosine [1] → ADA-SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency: no T, B or NK (natural killer) cells). PNP deficiency blocks inosine → hypoxanthine and guanosine → guanine [3] → T-cell deficiency only. Gout = too much end product, uric acid. Other steps: [2] 5′-nucleotidase, [4] guanase, [5] xanthine oxidase. Black bars mark the blocked steps. The top (PRPP → IMP) is de novo synthesis feeding in. BMT = bone marrow transplant; ERT = enzyme replacement therapy.

γc (common gamma chain) is a shared part of the receptors for several interleukins (immune growth signals). Without it, T and NK cells don't develop, and B cells are present but useless without T-cell help. Don't confuse (− = absent, + = present): X-SCID (X-linked) = T⁻ B⁺ NK⁻; ADA-SCID (autosomal recessive) = T⁻ B⁻ NK⁻, because dATP (deoxyadenosine triphosphate) poisons all lymphocytes.

ADA normally removes the amino group (red box) from deoxyadenosine, making deoxyinosine, which goes on to salvage or uric acid. Without ADA, deoxyadenosine builds up and kinases phosphorylate it: deoxyadenosine → dAMP → dADP → dATP (together, dAXP). The red arrow pointing up means these rise; the reaction itself runs from deoxyadenosine down to dATP. Excess dATP is toxic to lymphocytes (lymphotoxicity).

Correction: the counts are per µL (microliter), not per mL. dATP shuts off ribonucleotide reductase, the only enzyme that makes deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs, the DNA building blocks) from ribonucleotides. With no dNTPs, lymphocytes can't copy DNA or multiply, so both T cells (cell-mediated immunity) and B cells (antibodies, humoral immunity) fail.

Correction: PNP (purine nucleoside phosphorylase) splits a nucleoside (inosine, guanosine), not a nucleotide as the original slide says. It is step [3] (black bars): phosphorolysis breaks the base–sugar bond with inorganic phosphate instead of water, releasing the free base and ribose 1-phosphate. PNP deficiency is milder than ADA-SCID and hits mainly T cells. Without PNP, deoxyguanosine builds up and becomes dGTP, which is toxic to T cells (it may block ribonucleotide reductase). Fewer bases reach xanthine oxidase, so uric acid is low.

Answer: C. Low T, B and NK cells with low IgG = ADA-SCID, and ADA converts adenosine → inosine. E is the trap: ribonucleotide reductase is what dATP inhibits, not the defective enzyme. PNP deficiency would spare B cells and antibodies.

Unlike the purine ring, the pyrimidine ring is opened, so the end products are water-soluble (no crystal disease). Steps: nucleotide → nucleoside (nucleotidase) → free base (phosphorylase) → ring opened. Cytidine (labeled “Cytosine or Deoxycytosine”) is first deaminated to uridine, so cytosine follows uracil → β-alanine → malonyl CoA (→ acetyl CoA, so "ketogenic"). Thymine → β-aminoisobutyrate → methylmalonyl CoA → succinyl CoA (a citric acid cycle intermediate, so "glucogenic").

Hereditary orotic aciduria: UMP synthase (UMP = uridine monophosphate; the enzyme turns orotic acid into UMP) is defective. Orotic acid spills into the urine and cells run short of pyrimidines → megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate, plus growth retardation. Treatment: uridine, which is salvaged to UMP. Don't confuse with OTC (ornithine transcarbamylase) deficiency of the urea cycle: orotic aciduria too, but with high ammonia and no anemia.

qs.q: About what fraction of free purine bases is recycled by the salvage pathway?
qs.why: About 90% of purine bases are salvaged back to nucleotides; only about 10% are degraded to uric acid.

qs.q: Which enzyme removes the ribose from inosine to release hypoxanthine?
qs.why: PNP splits a nucleoside into its free base and ribose 1-phosphate. ADA acts one step earlier (adenosine → inosine), and 5′-nucleotidase removes the phosphate.

qs.q: Which metal is the key cofactor of xanthine oxidase?
qs.why: Xanthine oxidase contains molybdenum, with 2 FAD and 2 iron-sulfur centers carrying the electrons.

qs.q: In which tissues is uric acid mainly produced?
qs.why: Xanthine oxidase is concentrated in the liver and intestine. Other tissues have little of it, so their free bases are kept for salvage.

qs.q: HGPRT salvages which two purine bases?
qs.why: HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) turns hypoxanthine into IMP and guanine into GMP. Adenine is salvaged by a different enzyme, APRT.

qs.q: Why does active purine salvage slow de novo purine synthesis?
opts: It uses up glutamine needed for the first step
It uses up PRPP and makes inhibitory nucleotides
It raises PRPP, which inhibits the amidotransferase
It activates xanthine oxidase, draining IMP
qs.why: Salvage consumes PRPP, and the AMP, IMP and GMP it makes allosterically inhibit glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase, the committed step.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of hyperuricemia?
qs.why: Underexcretion by the kidneys causes over 90% of hyperuricemia. Overproduction (HGPRT deficiency, cancer, diet) is less common.

qs.q: What do gout crystals look like under polarized light?
qs.why: Monosodium urate crystals are needles with negative birefringence. Rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals are calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout).

qs.q: How is Lesch-Nyhan syndrome inherited?
qs.why: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (near-absent HGPRT) is X-linked recessive, so it is seen almost only in boys.

qs.q: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, what does allopurinol fail to correct?
opts: Orange urate crystals in the diaper
qs.why: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase and lowers uric acid, but the basal ganglia still lack salvage, so the neurological and self-injury symptoms remain.

qs.q: In von Gierke disease (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency), why is more purine made?
opts: HGPRT activity is lost, blocking salvage
Glucose 6-phosphate floods the HMP shunt, raising PRPP
qs.why: Trapped glucose 6-phosphate spills into the HMP (pentose phosphate) shunt, making more ribose 5-phosphate and PRPP, which drives purine synthesis. Trapping phosphate is hereditary fructose intolerance.

qs.q: How does heavy alcohol intake raise serum uric acid?
opts: Lactate competes with urate for renal excretion
Alcohol is metabolized into uric acid
qs.why: Alcohol raises lactate. In the proximal tubule, URAT1 swaps lactate (moving into the tubular fluid) for urate (moving out of the tubular fluid into the cell), so more lactate means more urate reabsorbed and less excreted.

qs.q: How does colchicine reduce gouty inflammation?
qs.why: Colchicine blocks microtubule assembly, so neutrophils cannot migrate into the joint or engulf crystals. Blocking cyclooxygenase is how NSAIDs work.

qs.q: Which cytokine, released by macrophages that take up urate crystals, draws neutrophils into the joint?
qs.why: Urate crystals switch on the pro-IL-1β gene; released IL-1β recruits neutrophils, which amplify the inflammation.

qs.q: What do colchicine, NSAIDs and steroids do to serum uric acid?
qs.why: These drugs only calm the acute flare; they do not change uric acid production or excretion.

qs.q: How does weight loss help lower serum urate?
opts: Lowers purine absorption in the gut
qs.why: Weight loss enhances the kidney's excretion of urate.

qs.q: How does allopurinol inhibit xanthine oxidase?
opts: By blocking URAT1 in the kidney
qs.why: Allopurinol is a purine (hypoxanthine) analog and a tight-binding competitive inhibitor: Km rises, Vmax stays the same. Non-competitive, non-purine describes febuxostat.

qs.q: Why can allopurinol affect pyrimidine-pathway enzymes while febuxostat cannot?
opts: Allopurinol resembles both purines and pyrimidines
Febuxostat is cleared before reaching cells
qs.why: Allopurinol and its metabolites are structural analogs of both purines and pyrimidines. Febuxostat is a non-purine that inhibits only xanthine oxidase.

qs.q: Why does blocking xanthine oxidase not cause crystals of xanthine and hypoxanthine?
opts: They are more soluble than uric acid
They are fully salvaged by APRT
They are degraded to malonyl CoA
They are bound to albumin in plasma
qs.why: Xanthine and hypoxanthine dissolve better than uric acid, so they can be salvaged or excreted without forming crystals.

qs.q: How does probenecid lower serum urate?
qs.why: Probenecid is a uricosuric: URAT1, on the apical membrane of the proximal tubule, normally moves urate out of the tubular fluid back into the cell (reabsorption); probenecid blocks it, so more urate stays in the urine and is excreted. It needs working kidneys to be useful.

qs.q: Which cells have the highest adenosine deaminase (ADA) activity?
qs.why: ADA is found in many tissues, but lymphocytes have the highest activity, which is why its loss hits the immune system.

qs.q: In ADA deficiency, which enzyme does the accumulating dATP inhibit?
qs.why: dATP shuts off ribonucleotide reductase, the enzyme that makes all dNTPs, so lymphocytes cannot copy DNA or divide.

qs.q: Which lymphocyte pattern fits X-linked SCID (loss of the common γ chain)?
qs.why: Without the common γ chain, T and NK cells don't develop; B cells are present but non-functional (− = absent, + = present). ADA-SCID is T⁻ B⁻ NK⁻.

qs.q: How is ADA-SCID inherited?
qs.why: ADA-SCID comes from autosomal recessive mutations in the ADA gene on chromosome 20. X-linked recessive is X-SCID, the most common type.

qs.q: What is the standard enzyme treatment for ADA deficiency?
qs.why: Frequent injections of PEG-ADA, a modified form of the ADA enzyme, are the standard treatment; bone marrow transplant and gene therapy are other options.

qs.q: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency mainly affects which cells?
qs.why: PNP deficiency is a milder immunodeficiency limited to T cells; B cells and antibodies are spared, unlike ADA-SCID.

qs.q: Which nucleotide is thought to build up and harm T cells in PNP deficiency?
qs.why: Without PNP, deoxyguanosine accumulates and becomes dGTP, which may inhibit ribonucleotide reductase. dATP is the toxic product in ADA deficiency.

qs.q: What happens to serum uric acid in PNP deficiency?
opts: Low, as fewer bases reach xanthine oxidase
High, from faster de novo synthesis
High, as more bases reach xanthine oxidase
qs.why: PNP releases the free bases that xanthine oxidase turns into uric acid. Without PNP, fewer bases are made, so uric acid is low.

qs.q: Thymine is degraded to which end product?
qs.why: Thymine → β-aminoisobutyrate → methylmalonyl CoA → succinyl CoA, a glucogenic product. Uracil and cytosine go to malonyl CoA (ketogenic).

qs.q: Hereditary orotic aciduria is a defect of which enzyme?
qs.why: UMP synthase turns orotic acid into UMP; when it fails, orotic acid spills into the urine and cells run short of pyrimidines.

qs.q: Which finding separates hereditary orotic aciduria from OTC deficiency?
opts: Low T cells with normal B cells
qs.why: Orotic aciduria causes megaloblastic anemia (not fixed by B12 or folate) without high ammonia. OTC deficiency also raises orotic acid but with high ammonia and no anemia.

slides.note: Diego and Jose are the same patient. Callos (tripe) and lengua (tongue) are organ meats; with red meat, they are among the richest sources of purines. Beer adds purines and alcohol. A sudden hot, swollen big-toe joint (first MTP, metatarsophalangeal, joint) is called podagra, the classic gout attack.

His BMI (body mass index = weight in kg ÷ height in m²) is 86 kg ÷ (1.80 m)² ≈ 26.5, overweight. Gout risk factors here: male sex, beer, extra weight, and a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol (the metabolic syndrome cluster, which goes with high uric acid).

Abnormal: uric acid 12 (high); creatinine 2.0 and BUN (blood urea nitrogen) 25 (both high, so the kidneys filter poorly); lactic acid 20 (slightly high); WBC 12,000 (mild rise from inflammation). Glucose, lipids and calcium are normal.

Correction: the synovial WBC count is 20,000 per µL (microliter), not per mL. Urine pH 5.0 is acidic. In acid urine, urate takes its uncharged uric acid form, which dissolves poorly, so acid urine favors uric acid stones, the kind that fits his past kidney stones. The synovial findings are explained under question 1d.

PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate) is activated ribose 5-phosphate. The ring is built on it: glutamine gives the first amino group (the committed step, PRPP amidotransferase), then glycine, aspartate, glutamine and THF (tetrahydrofolate, the folate form that carries one-carbon units) add the rest → IMP (inosine monophosphate; its base is hypoxanthine). AMP, IMP and GMP (left) and the allopurinol and 6-mercaptopurine nucleotides (right) inhibit the amidotransferase (⊖). IMP → GMP uses ATP and IMP → AMP uses GTP, which keeps the two balanced.

Drug targets: hydroxyurea blocks ribonucleotide reductase, which makes the deoxy (d) nucleotides used in DNA. 5-Fluorouracil blocks thymidylate synthase (dUMP → dTMP, the thymine nucleotide). Methotrexate, trimethoprim and pyrimethamine block DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase), which turns DHF (dihydrofolate) back into THF; without THF, no dTMP is made. Pyrimidines break down to soluble products, never uric acid.

Read left to right along the top, down the right side, then right to left along the bottom. CAD is one cytosolic protein carrying the first three enzymes (top row): CPS II (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II), ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase) and dihydroorotase. UMP synthase carries the last two steps (bottom row) and makes UMP (uridine monophosphate); its defect causes orotic aciduria. Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is the only mitochondrial step. UTP inhibits CPS II; ATP and PRPP activate it.

Breakdown goes in three moves: nucleotidases remove the phosphate, nucleoside phosphorylase removes the ribose (as ribose 1-phosphate), then the base is deaminated or oxidized on its way to uric acid. Adenine loses its amino group first (AMP → IMP or adenosine → inosine), so it ends as hypoxanthine. Guanine loses NH₄⁺ to become xanthine. Xanthine oxidase does hypoxanthine → xanthine → urate. Normally about 90% of freed hypoxanthine and guanine is salvaged back to nucleotides; only about 10% becomes uric acid.

Left chain, Lesch-Nyhan: without HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, the salvage enzyme), hypoxanthine and guanine can't be recycled. Unused PRPP piles up and activates the amidotransferase, while IMP and GMP fall, so there is less inhibition. De novo synthesis speeds up, and the extra purines are broken down → high uric acid. HGPRT also turns allopurinol and 6-mercaptopurine into the nucleotides that block this step.

Answers: 1a purine-rich food and beer raise production, and weak kidneys excrete too little urate. 1b Alcohol raises NADH, which turns pyruvate into lactate. 1c High creatinine and BUN mean a low GFR (eGFR 36). 1d Inflammatory fluid with urate crystals and no bacteria = gout. 1e Urate crystals → IL-1β → neutrophils flood the joint. 2 Tophi (urate lumps); xanthomas are cholesterol, and his lipids are normal. 3 Acute gouty arthritis on years of high uric acid. 4 Lactate makes URAT1 reabsorb more urate. 5 Now: steroids or low-dose colchicine (not NSAIDs); later: allopurinol or febuxostat and diet changes.

One clue settles each item. Trauma: a history of injury. Osteoarthritis: wear and tear, with no hot joint or fever. Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetric small joints of both hands, with morning stiffness. Septic arthritis: bacteria on Gram stain or culture of joint fluid (the dangerous one to rule out). Gout vs pseudogout: crystal shape in joint fluid. A hot big toe after a meat-and-beer feast points to gout.

Diego has both causes. Overproduction: organ meats and red meat are rich in nucleic acids, whose purines become uric acid, and beer adds more purines. Underexcretion: his kidneys filter poorly, and alcohol raises lactate. Why lactate: breaking down alcohol turns NAD⁺ into NADH (its reduced form). Excess NADH pushes lactate dehydrogenase to turn pyruvate into lactate, and lactate makes the kidney reabsorb more urate, so less is excreted (question 4).

Creatinine and urea are wastes cleared mainly by filtration, so when GFR (glomerular filtration rate, the plasma volume the kidneys filter per minute) falls, both build up in blood. eGFR (estimated GFR) is calculated from serum creatinine, age and sex; “per 1.73 m²” scales it to an average adult body size. His 36 is moderate chronic kidney disease (yellow zone). The kidneys excrete most of the body's uric acid, so with a low GFR he excretes less and it builds up in his blood.

20,000 WBC/µL, mostly neutrophils, means inflammatory fluid (normal is under 200; infection is usually over 50,000). Negative Gram stain and culture mean no bacteria, so not septic arthritis. Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis) are MSU (monosodium urate), so this is gout. Pseudogout crystals (calcium pyrophosphate) are rhomboid and weakly positive (blue when parallel).

Follow steps 1–5. Macrophages in the joint take up MSU crystals and switch on the gene for pro-IL-1β, which they activate and release as IL-1β (interleukin-1 beta, an inflammation signal). IL-1β calls neutrophils out of nearby vessels into the joint, and they release more inflammatory chemicals, so the joint becomes hot, red, swollen and painful. IL-1β also causes his fever and high blood WBC. Colchicine works at step 4 by stopping neutrophil migration.

Answer: tophi, lumps of MSU crystals walled off by inflammatory tissue. They form after years of high uric acid. Blood urate normally sits close to its saturation point, so at 12 mg/dL body fluids are supersaturated and crystals precipitate. Urate dissolves less as temperature falls, so cool spots (big toe, fingers, elbow, ear) collect crystals first. Tophi mean chronic gout.

Xanthomas are cholesterol-filled lumps in skin or tendons, seen with very high LDL (e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia). Diego's lipids are normal (total cholesterol 170, LDL 90), which argues against xanthoma. Xanthelasmas are yellow cholesterol plaques on the eyelids. Fluid drawn from a tophus shows urate crystals, which settles it.

Answer to question 3: Years of high uric acid, from weak kidney excretion (eGFR 36) plus a purine-rich, beer-heavy diet, left urate crystals in cool joints (tophi) and in the kidney (stones). The feast pushed uric acid and lactate higher. New crystals formed in the joints, and the neutrophil inflammation they set off caused the acute flare, with fever and a high WBC. Crystals seen in joint fluid confirm gout. HPI = history of present illness; PTC = prior to consultation; IP jt = interphalangeal joint; red ↑ = high; N = normal.

Tubule lumen (urine side, apical membrane) is on the right; blood side (basolateral membrane) is on the left. URAT1 moves urate out of the tubular fluid into the proximal tubule cell, and GLUT9 (glucose transporter 9) moves it out of the cell into the blood (arrows pointing left). This is reabsorption: urate is kept. In exchange, lactate moves from the cell into the tubular fluid, so more lactate drives more urate reabsorption. The listed drugs block URAT1 (uricosurics) but suit Diego poorly: they need good kidney function and raise the risk of uric acid stones.

His weak kidneys (eGFR 36) shape the choices. NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) block the prostaglandins that keep the afferent arteriole open, so they lower GFR further. Colchicine is cleared by the kidney, so it builds up and needs a lower dose. These drugs calm the flare but don't lower uric acid. Start allopurinol or febuxostat only after the flare settles (wait at least 2 weeks), because a sudden drop in urate can trigger new flares. Goal: urate below 6 mg/dL.

Uricase (urate oxidase) opens the purine ring of uric acid to make allantoin, which dissolves easily and is excreted. Humans lack a working uricase, so uric acid is our end product. Pegloticase is uricase given IV (into a vein). Its attached PEG (polyethylene glycol) chains make it less likely to trigger antibodies and keep it in blood longer. Allopurinol and febuxostat instead leave hypoxanthine and xanthine, which are more soluble than uric acid.

Why each step helps: less meat, organ meat, seafood and alcohol means fewer purines to break down and less lactate blocking urate excretion. Water dilutes the urine and lowers stone risk. Fructose is phosphorylated fast, using up ATP, and the extra AMP is broken down to uric acid.

qs.q: What is a sudden hot, swollen first metatarsophalangeal (big-toe) joint called?
qs.why: Podagra is the classic gout attack in the big-toe joint. A tophus is a chronic lump of urate crystals.

qs.q: Why do tripe and tongue (organ meats) raise serum uric acid?
qs.why: Organ meats and red meat are among the richest sources of purines, which are broken down to uric acid.

qs.q: High serum creatinine and high BUN together point to what?
qs.why: Creatinine and urea are cleared mainly by filtration, so both build up in blood when the kidneys filter poorly.

qs.q: Why does a urine pH of 5.0 favor uric acid kidney stones?
opts: Urate shifts to poorly soluble uric acid
Acid urine makes calcium oxalate dissolve
Urate stays in its soluble charged form
qs.why: In acid urine, urate picks up H⁺ and becomes uncharged uric acid, which dissolves poorly and forms stones.

qs.q: Methotrexate blocks dTMP synthesis by inhibiting which enzyme?
qs.why: Methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase, so DHF is not turned back into THF and the methylene-THF needed for dUMP → dTMP runs out. 5-Fluorouracil is the drug that blocks thymidylate synthase directly.

qs.q: How does pyrimidine ring assembly differ from purine ring assembly?
opts: Both rings are made free, then attached
Purine ring is made first, then attached to ribose-P
Pyrimidine ring is built step by step on PRPP
Pyrimidine ring is made first, then attached to ribose-P
qs.why: The pyrimidine ring is completed first (orotate) and then attached to ribose 5-phosphate from PRPP. The purine ring is built directly on activated ribose 5-phosphate.

qs.q: Which donor supplies atoms to the purine ring but not the pyrimidine ring?
qs.why: Glycine (and N¹⁰-formyl-THF) feeds only the purine ring. Aspartate, glutamine and CO₂ supply both rings.

qs.q: Which step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis takes place in the mitochondria?
qs.why: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is the only mitochondrial step. CPS II and aspartate transcarbamoylase are part of the cytosolic CAD protein, and UMP synthase is also cytosolic.

qs.q: How is guanine converted to xanthine?
qs.why: Guanine loses its amino group as NH₄⁺ to become xanthine. Xanthine oxidase acts on hypoxanthine and xanthine, not guanine.

qs.q: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (HGPRT deficiency), why does de novo purine synthesis speed up?
opts: Glutamine supply to the first step rises
PRPP builds up and IMP/GMP fall
qs.why: Unused PRPP activates the amidotransferase, and less IMP and GMP means less feedback inhibition, so more purines are made and broken down to uric acid.

qs.q: Which joint-fluid finding best separates gout from pseudogout?
qs.why: Gout crystals (monosodium urate) are needles; pseudogout crystals (calcium pyrophosphate) are rhomboid. Both cause inflammatory fluid.

qs.q: Which cause of an inflamed joint involves symmetric small joints of both hands with morning stiffness?
qs.why: Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune and typically symmetric in the small hand joints with morning stiffness. Osteoarthritis is wear and tear without a hot joint or fever.

qs.q: How does alcohol metabolism raise blood lactate?
opts: Raised NADH pushes pyruvate to lactate
Raised NAD⁺ pushes lactate to pyruvate
Alcohol is converted directly to lactate
qs.why: Breaking down alcohol turns NAD⁺ into NADH; excess NADH drives lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate to lactate.

qs.q: How does a low GFR (36 mL/min/1.73 m²) affect serum uric acid?
opts: Urate is retained, so it rises
The kidney makes more urate, so it rises
More urate is excreted, so it falls
No effect, as the liver clears urate
qs.why: The kidney excretes most uric acid, so poor filtration retains it, raising serum urate and favoring crystal deposition in joints.

qs.q: Joint fluid with 20,000 WBC/µL, mostly neutrophils, and a negative Gram stain and culture indicates what?
qs.why: 20,000 neutrophil-rich cells/µL is inflammatory fluid (normal is under 200), and no bacteria on stain or culture rules out septic arthritis.

qs.q: What causes the fever and high blood white cell count during an acute gout attack?
opts: Uric acid acting on the hypothalamus
IL-1β released in the inflamed joint
qs.why: Macrophages that take up urate crystals release IL-1β, which recruits neutrophils and also causes fever and a high blood WBC.

qs.q: Why do urate crystals deposit first in cool sites such as the big toe and ear?
opts: Urate dissolves less at warmer temperatures
Urate dissolves less at cooler temperatures
These joints bear the most weight
These joints have the most blood flow
qs.why: Urate solubility falls as temperature drops, so the coolest body parts collect crystals first.

qs.q: Which finding favors a xanthoma over a gouty tophus?
qs.why: Xanthomas are cholesterol deposits seen with very high LDL; tophi are urate deposits, often on earlobes, feet and elbows.

qs.q: What confirms the diagnosis of gout?
opts: Fever with a high WBC count
Urate crystals seen in joint fluid
A hot big toe after a feast
qs.why: Seeing needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid confirms gout; high uric acid alone does not.

qs.q: How does high lactate raise serum urate?
opts: Lactate blocks urate exit through GLUT9
URAT1 reabsorbs urate from the tubular fluid in exchange for lactate
URAT1 secretes urate into the tubular fluid in exchange for lactate
qs.why: URAT1, in the apical membrane of the proximal tubule, moves urate out of the tubular fluid into the cell (reabsorption) while lactate moves the other way, into the tubular fluid. More lactate drives more exchange, so more urate is kept and less is excreted.

qs.q: Why are NSAIDs avoided for an acute gout flare when eGFR is below 60?
opts: They block microtubules in the kidney
They need renal activation to work
They lower GFR by blocking prostaglandins
qs.why: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that keep the afferent arteriole open, so GFR falls further in weak kidneys.

qs.q: What does uricase (pegloticase) convert uric acid into?
qs.why: Uricase opens the purine ring of uric acid to make allantoin, which dissolves easily and is excreted. Humans lack a working uricase.

qs.q: Why does a high-fructose diet raise uric acid?
opts: Fast phosphorylation uses up ATP; extra AMP is degraded
Fructose inhibits purine salvage by HGPRT
Fructose blocks urate excretion by URAT1
Fructose is converted directly into uric acid
qs.why: Fructose is phosphorylated quickly, using up ATP; the extra AMP is broken down to uric acid.
